yugong.chinese_original:
Source: 列子・湯問篇 (Liezi, chapter 5), Chinese Wikisource, page 列子/湯問篇 (page id 12113), fetched 3 Oct 2026 through the Wikisource API. Full Yu Gong passage, copied exactly:

太行、王屋二山，方七百里，高萬仞，本在冀州之南，河陽之北。北山愚公者，年且九十，面山而居，懲山北之塞，出入之迂也，聚室而謀曰：「吾與汝畢力平險，指通豫南，達于漢陰，可乎？」雜然相許。其妻獻疑曰：「以君之力，曾不能損魁父之丘，如太行、王屋何？且焉置土石？」雜曰：「投諸渤海之尾，隱土之北。」遂率子孫荷擔者三夫，叩石墾壤，箕畚運於渤海之尾。鄰人京城氏之孀妻有遺男，始齔，跳往助之。寒暑易節，始一反焉。河曲智叟笑而止之，曰：「甚矣，汝之不惠！以殘年餘力，曾不能毀山之一毛，其如土石何？」北山愚公長息曰：「汝心之固，固不可徹，曾不若孀妻弱子。雖我之死，有子存焉；子又生孫，孫又生子；子又有子，子又有孫，子子孫孫無窮匱也，而山不加增，何苦而不平？」河曲智叟亡以應。操蛇之神聞之，懼其不已也，告之於帝。帝感其誠，命夸蛾氏二子負二山，一厝朔東，一厝雍南。自此，冀之南，漢之陰，無隴斷焉。

Spelling note: Wikisource writes 夸蛾氏 (insect radical). The Chinese school textbook and study sites write 夸娥氏 (woman radical). For Chinese captions, use 夸娥氏, because that is what viewers learned in school.

I did not use ctext.org. It blocked automated access with a security check and asked bots not to scrape it, so I did not try to get around that.
yugong.english_translation_source:
Lionel Giles (translator), "Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzu", Wisdom of the East series, London: John Murray, 1912. The story is in the chapter "The Questions of T'ang" (Book V), pages 86 to 88. The odd-page running head is "MOVING MOUNTAINS". Giles calls the hero "The Simpleton of the North Mountain", the mocker "The Wise Old Man of the River-bend" and the god "God Almighty".

I opened the archive.org full text (scan from University of California Libraries). The archive.org metadata gives Giles's dates as 1875-1958 and marks the book NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT for the US region. It is public domain in the US because it was published in 1912. In countries that protect a work for 70 years after the author's death (UK, EU), it stays in copyright until the end of 2028. I did not check Thai or Chinese copyright law in a source. Quoting a line or two in a Reel is a small use either way.

Clean-up done on the quotes: the text comes from OCR. I joined words split across lines ("addi- tion" became "addition"), took out the extra spaces before punctuation, and wrote "K'ua 0" as "K'ua O" (Giles's own footnote on the same page prints "K'ua O"). I made no other changes.

Things Giles leaves out or changes:
(1) 高萬仞 "ten thousand ren high" becomes just "an enormous altitude".
(2) He drops 豫南 "south of Yu" from the plan.
(3) He drops 隱土之北 "north of Yintu" from where the earth goes.
(4) He drops the family name 京城氏 (Jingcheng) of the widow and her boy.
(5) 曾不若孀妻弱子 "not even as good as the widow and her weak son" becomes "the widow's son" only.
(6) 魁父之丘, a small hill called Kuifu, becomes "a dunghill".
(7) 年且九十 "nearly ninety" becomes "an old man of ninety".
(8) 子孫荷擔者三夫 "three load-carrying men from his sons and grandsons" becomes "his son and grandson ... the three of them".
(9) He adds "Engrossed in their toil", which is not in the Chinese.
(10) 懼其不已也 becomes "fearing that it might never be finished". Chinese school notes read it as "afraid that he [Yu Gong] would never stop".
(11) 帝 becomes "God Almighty".
(12) 誠 "sincerity" becomes "simple faith".

I did not open A. C. Graham ("The Book of Lieh-tzu", 1960) or Lin Yutang. Neither is public domain, so do not quote them.

english_key_quotes.label: Opening: the mountains and the old man (Giles p. 86)
english_key_quotes.quote: The two mountains T'ai-hsing and Wang-wu, which cover an area of 700 square li, and rise to an enormous altitude, originally stood in the south of the Chi district and north of Ho-yang. The Simpleton of the North Mountain, an old man of ninety, dwelt opposite these mountains, and was vexed in spirit because their northern flanks blocked the way to travellers, who had to go all the way round.

english_key_quotes.label: The old man's plan (p. 86)
english_key_quotes.quote: So he called his family together, and broached a plan. "Let us," he said, "put forth our utmost strength to clear away this obstacle, and cut right through the mountains until we come to Han-yin. What say you?"

english_key_quotes.label: The wife's doubt (p. 86)
english_key_quotes.quote: They all assented except his wife, who made objections and said: "My goodman has not the strength to sweep away a dunghill, let alone two such mountains as T'ai-hsing and Wang-wu. Besides, where will you put all the earth and stones that you dig up?"

english_key_quotes.label: Where the earth goes, and the work begins (p. 86)
english_key_quotes.quote: The others replied that they would throw them on the promontory of P'o-hai. So the old man, followed by his son and grandson, sallied forth with their pickaxes, and the three of them began hewing away at the rocks, and cutting up the soil, and carting it away in baskets to the promontory of P'o-hai.

english_key_quotes.label: The neighbour's child (pp. 86-87)
english_key_quotes.quote: A widowed woman who lived near had a little boy who, though he was only just shedding his milk teeth, came skipping along to give them what help he could.

english_key_quotes.label: How long one trip took (p. 87)
english_key_quotes.quote: Engrossed in their toil, they never went home except once at the turn of the season.

english_key_quotes.label: The Wise Old Man's mockery (p. 87)
english_key_quotes.quote: The Wise Old Man of the River-bend burst out laughing and urged them to stop. "Great indeed is your witlessness!" he said. "With the poor remaining strength of your declining years you will not succeed in removing a hair's breadth of the mountain, much less the whole vast mass of rock and soil."

english_key_quotes.label: The old man's reply: sons and grandsons, the mountain does not grow (p. 87)
english_key_quotes.quote: With a sigh, the Simpleton of the North Mountain replied: "Surely it is you who are narrow-minded and unreasonable. You are not to be compared with the widow's son, despite his puny strength. Though I myself must die, I shall leave a son behind me, and through him a grandson. That grandson will beget sons in his turn, and those sons will also have sons and grandsons. With all this posterity, my line will not die out, while on the other hand the mountain will receive no increment or addition. Why then should I despair of levelling it to the ground at last?"

english_key_quotes.label: The mocker has no answer (p. 87)
english_key_quotes.quote: The Wise Old Man of the River-bend had nothing to say in reply.

english_key_quotes.label: The ending: the gods move the mountains (pp. 87-88)
english_key_quotes.quote: One of the serpent-brandishing deities heard of the undertaking and, fearing that it might never be finished, went and told God Almighty, who was touched by the old man's simple faith, and commanded the two sons of K'ua O to transport the mountains, one to the extreme north-east, the other to the southern corner of Yung.

english_key_quotes.label: Giles's footnote on K'ua O (p. 88)
english_key_quotes.quote: K'ua O was apparently a god of strength.

english_key_quotes.label: Last line (p. 88)
english_key_quotes.quote: Ever since then, the region lying between Chi in the north and Han in the south has been an unbroken plain.

yugong.story_facts:
Each fact is tied to the Chinese words from Wikisource 列子/湯問篇. The school notes I mention come from Chinese study sites (ixuehai.cn, 21cnjy.com) that I read through a summary tool. Check the printed textbook before you quote those notes word for word.

1. HIS NAME. 北山愚公 = "the Foolish Old Man of North Mountain". 愚 means foolish or simple. Giles calls him "The Simpleton of the North Mountain".

2. HIS AGE. 年且九十 = "nearly ninety". 且 means "almost" (school note: 將近). He was not quite ninety yet.

3. THE TWO MOUNTAINS. 太行、王屋二山 = Taihang and Wangwu. Giles spells the first one "T'ai-hsing". The modern name is Taihang.

4. HOW BIG. 方七百里 = 700 li "square" (the school note says 方 means area). 高萬仞 = ten thousand ren high. A ren is an old unit of 7 or 8 chi. Giles gives "700 square li" but only "an enormous altitude" for the height.

5. WHERE THE MOUNTAINS STOOD. 本在冀州之南，河陽之北 = south of Jizhou, north of Heyang.

6. WHY HE WANTED TO MOVE THEM. 面山而居，懲山北之塞，出入之迂也 = his house faced the mountains. They blocked the north side, so every trip out and back took the long way round.

7. THE PLAN. 聚室而謀 = he called the whole family together to plan. 吾與汝畢力平險，指通豫南，達于漢陰 = "Let us use all our strength to flatten the hard place, and open a straight road to south of Yu and on to the south bank of the Han river." 雜然相許 = everyone agreed.

8. THE WIFE. 其妻獻疑 = his wife "offered a doubt". She asks questions, she does not laugh at him. 以君之力，曾不能損魁父之丘 = "With your strength you could not even make the little Kuifu hill smaller." 且焉置土石 = "And where will you put the earth and stones?"

9. WHERE THE EARTH WENT. 投諸渤海之尾，隱土之北 = "Throw it at the tail (far edge) of the Bohai Sea, north of Yintu." 箕畚運於渤海之尾 = they carried it in baskets (箕畚) to the edge of the Bohai Sea.

10. WHO DUG. 遂率子孫荷擔者三夫 = he led three men from his sons and grandsons who could carry loads. The Chinese can be read two ways. Giles counts the old man as one of the three.

11. THE WORK. 叩石墾壤 = they broke stones and dug the soil.

12. THE CHILD HELPER. 鄰人京城氏之孀妻有遺男，始齔，跳往助之 = a neighbour, a widow of the Jingcheng (京城) family, had a son whose father had died. He had 始齔, just started to lose his baby teeth (school note: about 7 or 8 years old). He came 跳往, jumping and skipping, to help.

13. HOW LONG ONE TRIP TOOK. 寒暑易節，始一反焉 = winter and summer changed places before they came back even once. One trip to the sea and back took a whole change of season (school translation: 冬夏換季，才往返一次). Giles reads it as "they never went home except once at the turn of the season".

14. THE MOCKER. 河曲智叟 = the Wise Old Man of the River Bend (智 = clever). 笑而止之 = he laughed and tried to stop them. 甚矣，汝之不惠 = "How very unwise you are!" 以殘年餘力，曾不能毀山之一毛，其如土石何 = "With the few years and the little strength you have left, you can't break even one hair of this mountain. What can you do about all that earth and stone?"

15. THE REPLY. 北山愚公長息曰 = the Foolish Old Man gave a long sigh. 汝心之固，固不可徹，曾不若孀妻弱子 = "Your mind is so shut that nothing can get in. You are not even as good as the widow and her small boy." 雖我之死，有子存焉；子又生孫，孫又生子；子又有子，子又有孫，子子孫孫無窮匱也 = "Even when I die, my son is still here. My son has grandsons, the grandsons have sons, and on and on. Sons and grandsons never run out." 而山不加增，何苦而不平 = "But the mountain does not get any bigger. So why worry that it will never be flat?"

16. THE MOCKER IS SILENT. 河曲智叟亡以應 = the Wise Old Man had no answer.

17. THE SNAKE-HOLDING GOD. 操蛇之神聞之，懼其不已也，告之於帝 = the god who holds snakes heard about it (school note: a mountain god with snakes in his hands). He was afraid the old man would never stop (school note: 其 = 愚公, 已 = stop). He told 帝, the god of the sky (school note: 天帝).

18. WHY THE SKY GOD HELPED. 帝感其誠 = the sky god was moved by his 誠, his sincerity, his true heart.

19. WHO CARRIED THE MOUNTAINS. 命夸蛾氏二子負二山 = he ordered the two sons of Kua'e (school text 夸娥氏; school note: a god of great strength) to carry the two mountains on their backs (負). The old man did not finish the job himself.

20. WHERE THEY PUT THEM. 一厝朔東，一厝雍南 = one was put east of Shuo (school note: east of Shuofang, in the far north), the other south of Yong (Yongzhou). Giles: "one to the extreme north-east, the other to the southern corner of Yung".

21. THE ENDING. 自此，冀之南，漢之陰，無隴斷焉 = from then on, from south of Ji down to the south bank of the Han, no high ground blocked the way.

22. THE JOKE IN THE NAMES. The "Foolish" old man (愚公) turns out to be wise, and the "Wise" old man (智叟) is the one with no answer.

23. ASANA LINK. No asana is named after this story. It comes from a Chinese Daoist book, not an Indian or yoga text. In "Hidden Stories of Ashtanga", the bridge has to be the lesson (small work every day adds up), not a claim that an asana comes from this story.
yugong.bedtime_version: Long ago, the Foolish Old Man, almost ninety years old, lived in front of two huge mountains. The mountains blocked his road, so every trip took the long way round. One day he said to his family, "Let us flatten the mountains and make a straight road." His wife asked, "You can't even move a little hill, so where will you put all that earth and stone?" "We will carry it to the edge of the far sea," the family said. So he and his sons and grandsons broke stones, dug the earth, and carried it away in baskets. A little neighbour boy, just losing his baby teeth, came skipping over to help. The sea was so far away that one trip there and back took a whole season. A man called the Wise Old Man laughed and said, "You are so old, you can't move one tiny bit of this mountain!" The Foolish Old Man sighed and said, "When I am gone, my children will dig, then their children, and their children, but the mountain will never get any bigger." The Wise Old Man had nothing to say. The mountain god who holds snakes heard this, and he worried that the old man would never stop. He told the great god of the sky, who was moved by the old man's true heart and sent two very strong sons of the Kua'e family to carry the mountains far away on their backs. From that day on, the road was flat and open.
yugong.common_errors:
1. "He was 90." The text says 年且九十, "nearly ninety". Giles also says "of ninety". Say "almost ninety".

2. "He dug until the mountains were gone." Wrong. Two strong sons of Kua'e (夸娥氏) carried the mountains away on their backs. The lesson is that his steady, true work moved the gods. He did not finish it himself.

3. "The god felt sorry for him" or "rewarded hard work". The text gives two reasons. The snake-holding god was afraid the old man would never stop (懼其不已也), and the sky god was moved by his sincerity (帝感其誠). Giles's "fearing that it might never be finished" is a different reading from the Chinese school notes.

4. "One round trip between the mountain and his home took a year." English Wikipedia says this. The text says the trip to the Bohai Sea and back took a change of season (寒暑易節，始一反焉). Do not say "a year" as if it were fact.

5. Wikipedia also says he took a food called "Chaoqi". That is not in the Liezi text.

6. The wife mocking him. She 獻疑, "offers a doubt", and asks a fair question: where will the earth go? The mocker is a different man, the Wise Old Man of the River Bend (河曲智叟). Do not merge the two.

7. "His grandson helped." The child helper is a neighbour: the widow's son from the Jingcheng family, about 7 or 8 (始齔). He is not family.

8. "The gods in Heaven ordered the mountains split apart." Also in Wikipedia, and wrong. One sky god (帝) gave the order. The two mountains were carried away whole, one to the east of Shuo and one to the south of Yong.

9. Calling the god the "Jade Emperor". The text only says 帝, and the school note says 天帝. In English, say "the god of the sky". Do not use "emperor" or "king", which also keeps us clear of the royalty rule.

10. Mixing up 夸娥氏 with 夸父. Kuafu is the giant who chased the sun and died of thirst. That is the very next story in the same chapter, and it is not this one.

11. Dating claims like "2,400 years old" or "4th century BC". Giles himself writes that the book "has evidently passed through the hands of many editors and gathered numerous accretions". Say "an old Chinese book called the Liezi" and give no age.

12. Spelling. Giles writes "T'ai-hsing". The modern name is Taihang (太行).

13. "Dunghill" is Giles's own word. The Chinese is 魁父之丘, a small hill called Kuifu. For a family audience, say "a little hill".

14. Making Yu Gong truly stupid. The point of the names is that "Foolish" (愚) is wise and "Wise" (智) is the fool.

15. Claiming an asana link. No asana is named after Yu Gong, and the story is not Indian or yogic. Do not say "this asana comes from this story". The closest Indian story with the same shape (a small creature, a huge task, a god steps in) is the tittibha bird and the sea (Tittibhasana), which is already used.

16. Pulling from nearby stories. The same Tang Wen chapter has stories with death and with eating children (輒沐之國). The Yu Gong passage itself has no violent or adult parts. Only the word "widow" hints at a death, which is fine for a bedtime story.
yugong.china_channel_risk:
VERDICT: Low risk, if we tell the old Liezi fable as a story about patience and small daily work, and never give it a political meaning.

WHY IT IS SAFE: Every Chinese adult learned this story at school. It is a lesson in the national Chinese textbook (部編/統編版, Grade 8, first term, Unit 6). One study site says lesson 24 in the 2022-23 printing (zy.21cnjy.com/13631846). Another says lesson 22 (ixuehai.cn/html/1327.html). Both are secondary sites, so check before quoting a lesson number. The school reading is about never giving up, which matches Boonchu's message of "little techniques every day".

WHERE THE RISK IS: The risk is in how we frame it, not in the story. English Wikipedia (which I opened) says Mao Zedong retold it in a speech at Yan'an on 11 June 1945. In that speech the two mountains became political enemies, and the "God" in the story became the people. The speech was one of the "Three Constantly Read Articles" in the Cultural Revolution. Many older Chinese viewers will think of that speech when they hear 愚公移山.

NEVER SAY OR WRITE: Mao, the speech, Yan'an, the Party, the Cultural Revolution, or any leader. Avoid any re-reading of the two mountains as something "pressing on the people". Avoid these words: "the people are God", "the masses", "imperialism", "feudalism", "revolution", "overthrow", "struggle", "fight the system". Do not tie it to any slogan. The phrase is also used in public and official language in China, but I did not check specific cases, so do not echo any of them.

ALSO AVOID:
(1) Jokes, parody or wordplay on the title 愚公移山. It is a school classic and carries political memory.
(2) Calling anyone "愚" (foolish).
(3) Saying it is an Indian or yoga story, or that an asana comes from it. Chinese viewers know it well and will spot the mistake.
(4) Getting the details wrong. Viewers studied 年且九十, 夸娥氏, 操蛇之神 and 渤海之尾 at school.

SAFE FRAMING: An old man, his family and a little neighbour boy, carrying one basket at a time. Each basket seems small, but they never stop. In Chinese captions, use 天帝 for the god, as the textbook does. In English, say "the god of the sky", never "emperor" or "king". Keep it about practice, patience and family.

yugongCheck.story_errors:
1. BEDTIME, wrong length of time: "one trip there and back took a whole season" is too short. The Chinese is 寒暑易節，始一反焉. Both school sites the report cites read it as about one year. ixuehai: 指一年的时间. 21cnjy: 冬夏换季(即一年). Fix: "The sea was so far away that winter turned to summer before they got back from just one trip."
2. COMMON ERROR #4 is itself wrong. "A year" is the standard school reading, not a mistake. Wikipedia's real slips are "between the mountain and his home" (the trip was to the Bohai Sea and back) and "Chaoqi". Also, the report puts a paraphrase in quote marks as if it were Wikipedia's wording. The real wording is in corrected_quote. Fact 13 should also add the school note "about a year".
3. BEDTIME, wife's line: "You can't even move a little hill, so where will you put all that earth and stone?" This joins two separate questions with a "so" that does not follow, and it drops her real point (how can you move two big mountains?). Fix: His wife asked, "You are not strong enough to move even a little hill. How can you move two big mountains? And where will you put all the earth and stone?"
4. BEDTIME leaves out the theme line. 而山不加增，何苦而不平 means "the mountain will not grow, so why worry that it will never be flat?" Add after "never get any bigger": "So why should I worry that it will never be flat?"
5. BEDTIME: "two very strong sons of the Kua'e family". The text says 夸娥氏二子, and the school note says 夸娥氏 is the god of great strength (school translation: 大力神夸娥氏的两个儿子). Fix: "the two sons of Kua'e, a very strong god".
6. FACT 20: "(school note: east of Shuofang, in the far north)". The ixuehai note says 朔方以东地区，指山西省的东部 (eastern Shanxi). "In the far north" is not in that note. Giles says "the extreme north-east". Drop "in the far north".
7. FACT 14: "can't break even one hair of this mountain". The school note reads 一毛 as 一草一木, "not even one blade of grass on the mountain". Giles says "a hair's breadth". This is a minor gloss issue.
8. FACT 15: "My son has grandsons" is wrong. 子又生孫 means my son will have a son (my grandson). Then 孫又生子: the grandson will have a son.
9. FACT 10: "The Chinese can be read two ways" overstates the doubt. The school translation is clear: 愚公率领儿孙中能挑担子的三个人, three load-carriers from among his sons and grandsons, led by the old man. Giles's "the three of them" counts the old man, which is his own loose reading.
10. COMMON ERROR #8: Wikipedia says "ordered the mountains separated", not "split apart".
11. GILES CHANGES LIST, incomplete: Giles also adds "travellers" (the Chinese 出入之迂 means the old man's own trips in and out) and "pickaxes" (no tool is named except 箕畚 baskets). These are not errors in the report, but add them if Giles is quoted on screen.
12. CHECKED AND CORRECT: all 23 facts not listed above, the 12 Giles-omission notes, Giles 1875-1958, the end-2028 UK/EU copyright date, Kuafu being the next story (Wikisource line 5), 輒沐之國 child-eating in the same chapter (line 11), and the Mao speech facts (Yan'an, 11 June 1945, "Our God is none other than the masses of the Chinese people", Three Constantly Read Articles, Cultural Revolution), all confirmed on English Wikipedia.
yugongCheck.safety: The Yu Gong passage itself is safe for a bedtime story. It has no violence or adult content. "Widow" (孀妻) only hints at a death, and the bedtime version already drops it. Keep out the rest of the Tang Wen chapter. Kuafu dying of thirst is the very next paragraph, and the 輒沐之國 passage about eating firstborn children is a few paragraphs later. Both are confirmed in the Wikisource text. The China-channel note is accurate and contains nothing false: the story is in the 部编版 Grade 8 textbook, Unit 6, and Mao's 1945 Yan'an speech re-read the two mountains as imperialism and feudalism and God as the masses. Keep its rules: no Mao, Party, speech, leaders, slogans or "struggle" words; no parody of the title 愚公移山; 帝 = "the god of the sky" (Chinese caption 天帝), never "emperor" or "king". No royalty or monarchy content. Nothing mocks a god or a religion. One small point: the textbook body text writes 帝. 天帝 comes from the school note, not the body text.
yugongCheck.plain_note_for_boonchu: The old Chinese text and every English line from Giles match the books word for word. Fix a few small things in the bedtime story: one trip to the sea took about a year, not one season, and add the old man's best line, "The mountain will not grow, so why worry?" No asana comes from this story, so link it to daily practice, not to an asana name.

asanas.name: Kurmasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Bhuja Pidasana. After: Supta Kurmasana. The two are one flow: Supta Kurmasana goes on from vinyasa 8 straight out of Kurmasana. Order checked on the ashtangayoga.info Primary page and its Primary cheat sheet PDF. I could not open Yoga Mala, Anusthana, Miele or Maehle: the archive.org copies are lend-only.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: kurma = 'a tortoise, turtle' (Monier-Williams, MW p. 300). MW also says: 'Viṣṇu's second incarnation (descent in the form of a tortoise to support the mountain Mandara at the churning of the ocean)'. So the tortoise held a whole mountain on its back. This is a strong link to the mountain theme. Bedtime flag: leave out the poison and the fight over the nectar that come later in the churning story. MW: https://www.sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/csl-apidev/getword.php?dict=mw&key=kUrma&input=slp1&output=iast

asanas.name: Supta Kurmasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Kurmasana. After: Garbha Pindasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: supta = 'fallen asleep, slept, sleeping, asleep' and 'lain down to sleep' (MW p. 1230). kurma = tortoise. So: the sleeping tortoise.

asanas.name: Hanumanasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Ganda Bherundasana. After: Supta Trivikramasana. Sources do not fully agree. The ashtangayoga.info Third series web page and Matthew Sweeney's list (copied on a blog) put Hanumanasana first, then Supta Trivikramasana. The ashtangayoga.info Advanced A cheat sheet PDF puts Supta Trivikramasana (no. 25) before Hanumanasana (no. 26). Check your own Mysore notes before you say the order on camera.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: hanu-mat = 'having (large) jaws', the name of the monkey chief (MW p. 1288). MW says he 'is fabled to have assumed any form at will, wielded rocks, removed mountains, mounted the air, seized the clouds'. This is a new mountain angle. Flag: the famous story of Hanuman carrying the herb mountain happens inside the Rama and Ravana war, so keep the war out. Hanuman and Surasa is already used. The ashtangayoga.info Hanumanasana page (Steiner's retelling, a secondary source) also tells of Mainaka, a mountain that rises from the sea so Hanuman can rest. MW: https://www.sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/csl-apidev/getword.php?dict=mw&key=hanumat&input=slp1&output=iast

asanas.name: Trivikramasana (Utthita Trivikramasana)
asanas.position_note: Before: Digasana B. After: Natarajasana. It starts and ends in Samasthitih (ashtangayoga.info item page). Same order on the ashtangayoga.info cheat sheet and on Sweeney's list.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: tri = three. vikrama = 'a step, stride, pace' (MW p. 955). trivikrama = 'the 3 steps (of Viṣṇu)' and 'who strided over the 3 worlds in 3 steps (Viṣṇu)' (MW p. 460). A tiny dwarf (Vamana) grows huge and covers the world in three steps, so it fits the small-to-big theme. Flag: the story ends with Bali, an Asura king, pushed down to the underworld. That is a king and a fight, so tell it softly or leave that ending out.

asanas.name: Supta Trivikramasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Hanumanasana. After: Digasana A. See the order note under Hanumanasana: one ashtangayoga.info cheat sheet swaps these two.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: supta = lying down, asleep (MW p. 1230). trivikrama = Vishnu who took the 3 great steps (MW p. 460). So: Trivikrama lying down.

asanas.name: Bharadvajasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Bakasana B. After: Ardha Matsyendrasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: Bharad-vaja = 'bearing speed or strength (of flight)', a skylark. It is also the name of a Rishi, the author of many Rig Veda hymns (MW p. 747). Already scripted on 29 Sep (the three mountains of the Vedas) but never filmed.

asanas.name: Ardha Matsyendrasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Bharadvajasana. After: Eka Pada Sirsasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: ardha = 'half' (MW p. 91). matsya = 'a fish'. indra at the end of a word = 'the chief'. matsyendra = 'N. of a teacher of Yoga' (MW p. 776). So: the half twist of Matsyendra, the lord of the fishes.

asanas.name: Purna Matsyendrasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Ashtavakrasana B. After: Viranchyasana A.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: purna = 'filled, full', 'complete, all, entire' (MW p. 642). matsyendra = the yoga teacher, lord of the fishes. ashtangayoga.info (secondary) tells that a fish heard Shiva teach yoga to Parvati and became the yogi Matsyendra. A gentle story with no flags.

asanas.name: Vishvamitrasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Vasishthasana (first asana of the series). After: Kashyapasana. Note: ashtangayoga.info says older Ashtanga books swap the names of Vasishthasana and Vishvamitrasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: vishva-mitra = '(prob.) friend of all', a famous Rishi (MW p. 994). Already used (Vishvamitra losing tapas and starting again). Flag: he was a king first, and he had a rivalry with Vasishtha.

asanas.name: Kashyapasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Vishvamitrasana. After: Chakorasana. It is the first of the leg-behind-the-head group, done lying on the back.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: kashyapa = 'having black teeth'. It also means 'a tortoise (kacchapa)'. It is the name of an ancient sage, husband of Aditi and father of the Adityas, and father of Vishnu 'in his vAmana avatAra' (MW p. 265). Note the tortoise link to Kurmasana and the dwarf link to Trivikramasana.

asanas.name: Galavasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Urdhva Kukkutasana C. After: Eka Pada Bakasana A.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: galava = a tree (Symplocos racemosa) and 'a kind of ebony'. It is also the name of 'an old sage and preceptor (son [Hariv.] or pupil [MBh.] of Viśvā-mitra)' (MW p. 354). Flag: the Mahabharata Galava story (800 horses, the princess Madhavi given to kings) is adult and full of kings. Leave it out of a bedtime story.

asanas.name: Kaundinyasana (A and B)
asanas.position_note: Before: Eka Pada Bakasana B. After: Ashtavakrasana A.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: kaundinya = a family name, 'son of the line of Kundina'. Also an old grammarian, and 'one of the 24 mythical Buddhas' (MW p. 315). Flag: the best-known legend (on ashtangayoga.info) is about starting a royal line in Funan (old Cambodia) by marrying a Naga princess. It is royal, so do not use it.

asanas.name: Durvasasana
asanas.position_note: Often spelled Durvasana on Ashtanga charts. Before: Skandasana. After: Urdhva Kukkutasana A.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: dur-vasas = 'badly clad, naked'. It is the name of a Rishi, son of Atri and Anasuya, 'thought to be an incarnation of Śiva, known for his irascibility' (MW p. 487). In plain words, a sage who got angry fast. Flag: his stories are full of curses. Do not mock him.

asanas.name: Skandasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Bhairavasana. After: Durvasasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: skanda = 'anything which jumps or hops'. It also means 'Attacker', the name of Karttikeya, son of Shiva, called the 'god of war' (MW p. 1256). Flag: war god. If used, stay with 'the one who leaps'.

asanas.name: Bhairavasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Chakorasana. After: Skandasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: bhairava = 'frightful, terrible, horrible, formidable', the name of a fierce form of Shiva (MW p. 767). MW also lists 'a mountain' (found only in old word lists). Flag: the main story (told on ashtangayoga.info from the Kurma Purana) has Shiva cut off one of Brahma's heads. It is violent, so leave it out.

asanas.name: Viranchyasana (A and B)
asanas.position_note: Before: Purna Matsyendrasana. After: Dvi Pada Viparita Dandasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: viranca, viranci, virancya = names of Brahma, the creator (MW p. 982). ashtangayoga.info also gives 'the even-minded one', but that meaning is not in MW.

asanas.name: Garbha Pindasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Supta Kurmasana. After: Kukkutasana. You roll around in a circle 9 times (per the cheat sheet), then roll up into Kukkutasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: garbha = 'the womb' and 'a foetus or embryo' (MW p. 349). pinda = 'any round or roundish mass or heap, a ball', and also 'the embryo in an early stage' (MW p. 625). So: a baby curled up like a ball in the womb.

asanas.name: Kukkutasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Garbha Pindasana. After: Baddha Konasana A.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: kukkuta = 'a cock', 'a wild cock' (MW p. 287). So: the rooster.

asanas.name: Bhekasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Shalabhasana B. After: Dhanurasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: bheka = 'a frog' (MW p. 766). MW adds a small story from the Kathasaritsagara: frogs croak because of a curse from Agni, after they told the gods where he was hiding in the water.

asanas.name: Krounchasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Pashasana (first asana of the series). After: Shalabhasana A.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: krauncha = 'a kind of curlew' (a long-legged water bird) (MW p. 323). MW also gives it as the name of a mountain in the Himalaya, 'said to have been split by Kārttikeya'. That is a mountain link, but splitting it with a spear is violent. Flag: the famous Valmiki krauncha story has a hunter kill a bird. Leave both out of a bedtime version.

asanas.name: Nakrasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Mayurasana. After: Vatayanasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: nakra = 'crocodile, alligator' (MW p. 524).

asanas.name: Karandavasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Pincha Mayurasana. After: Mayurasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: karandava = karanda = 'a sort of duck' (MW p. 274).

asanas.name: Mayurasana
asanas.position_note: Before: Karandavasana. After: Nakrasana.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: mayura = 'a peacock' (MW p. 789). MW also lists Mayura as the name of a mountain.

asanas.name: Parvatasana
asanas.series: None in the current KPJAYI charts (Primary, Intermediate, Advanced A, Advanced B). It only shows up in an old Advanced D (sixth series) list.
asanas.position_note: It is not on the ashtangayoga.info charts or on Kino MacGregor's Advanced B list. A blog list of the old Advanced C and D (based on David Swenson's DVD) ends with 'Parvatasana A B'. The same blog says that list 'is not the same as what is being taught now in Mysore'. In Iyengar and other schools it is a seated lotus with the arms up (secondary sources only).
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: parvata = 'a mountain, mountain-range, height, hill, rock'. As an adjective it means 'knotty, rugged (said of mountains)' (MW p. 609). It is the plainest word for mountain. MW: https://www.sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/csl-apidev/getword.php?dict=mw&key=parvata&input=slp1&output=iast

asanas.name: Agastyasana
asanas.position_note: Not on any Ashtanga chart I opened. Yoga Vidya (a Sivananda-line school) lists Agasthiyarasana as a kind of Ardha Matsyendrasana twist, dedicated to the sage Agastya.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: agasti / agastya: MW says it comes 'fr. 2. a-ga, a mountain, and asti, thrower' (from the Unadi Sutra), so 'mountain-thrower'. MW: a sage 'born in a water-jar', 'of short stature', who 'swallowed the ocean, and compelled the Vindhya mountains to prostrate themselves before him' (MW p. 4). This is the best mountain myth I found, but no Ashtanga asana is named after him. Flag: the ocean-swallowing ties to a fight with demons. The Vindhya part is gentle. MW: https://www.sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/csl-apidev/getword.php?dict=mw&key=agasti&input=slp1&output=iast

asanas.name: Bhagirathasana
asanas.position_note: Not on any Ashtanga chart. Some teachers use it as another name for Vrikshasana (tree). One blog says Krishnamacharya gave it this name, but the blog cites no source and contradicts itself. Do not repeat that claim.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: Bhagiratha = 'prob. fr. bhagin + ratha, having a glorious chariot', an ancient king who 'brought down the sacred Gaṅgā from heaven to earth' (MW p. 744). The theme fit is strong: years of patient effort over many generations. But he is a king (this breaks the royalty rule), and the story is about the ashes of the 60,000 dead sons of Sagara. Flag both.

asanas.name: Samasthitih
asanas.series: All series (the standing start and end position)
asanas.position_note: After the opening chant you stand in Samasthitih. Then Surya Namaskara A starts (vinyasa 1, breathe in, arms up). You come back to it at the end of each sun salutation and between the standing asanas. Every series starts and ends here.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: sama = 'even, smooth, flat, plain, level', 'same, equal' and 'having the right measure, regular, normal, right, straight' (MW p. 1152). sthiti = 'standing upright or firmly, not falling' (MW p. 1264). So: standing even and steady. MW has no entry for the joined word. ashtangayoga.info gives 'standing upright'.

asanas.name: Tadasana
asanas.series: Advanced B (Fourth series), as its own asana
asanas.position_note: Before: Marichyasana H. After: Samanasana. This is on Kino MacGregor's Advanced B page, and Matthew Sweeney's list (copied on a blog) has the same order. In the other series the standing start is called Samasthitih, not Tadasana. Wikipedia (citing Ramaswami 2005, a secondary source) says that in Ashtanga Tadasana is done on the toes and Samasthitih is done flat-footed.
asanas.sanskrit_meaning: tada = 'a blow'. It also means 'a mountain' (MW p. 441). MW marks that meaning 'L.', which means it is found only in old word lists. So Tadasana = the mountain asana. MW: https://www.sanskrit-lexicon.uni-koeln.de/scans/csl-apidev/getword.php?dict=mw&key=tAqa&input=slp1&output=iast

candidates.myth_title: The Tortoise Who Held the Mountain (the churning of the milk ocean)
candidates.asana: Kurmasana and Supta Kurmasana. Extra hooks if wanted: Kasyapasana (the churners are all sons of Kashyapa) and Durvasasana (Durvasa's curse starts the story in Vishnu Purana 1.9).
candidates.series_claim: Primary. In K. Pattabhi Jois's Yoga Mala (English ed., North Point Press), Kurmasana is asana no. 22 of the Primary list, and Supta Kurmasana is named there as the state of its 9th vinyasa. It is also on the Primary list at grimmly1997.blogspot.com (copied from Ashtanga Diary). Kasyapasana and Durvasasana are on the Advanced A list on the same page (from Matthew Sweeney's Astanga Yoga As It Is), which is a secondary source.
candidates.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva, sections 17 and 18, tr. K. M. Ganguli (1883 to 1896), Project Gutenberg eBook 15474. Sanskrit critical edition 1.16.10 to 11 and 1.16.28 to 29 (GRETIL). Vishnu Purana 1.9, tr. H. H. Wilson (1840), on wisdomlib. Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda Canto XLV 'The Quest of the Amrit', tr. R. T. H. Griffith (1870 to 1874), Gutenberg eBook 24869. Bhagavata Purana 2.7.13, 5.18.30, 8.7.7 to 8.7.19, 8.8.1 and 8.8.31 to 35, Sanskrit only (GRETIL). I found no public-domain English Bhagavata to quote, so any Bhagavata wording below is my own rough gloss. Bridge text: Liezi chapter 5, Tang Wen, Chinese text on zh.wikisource.
candidates.key_quote: "The gods then went to the king of tortoises and said to him, 'O Tortoise-king, thou wilt have to hold the mountain on thy back!' The Tortoise-king agreed, and Indra contrived to place the mountain on the former's back." And, from the same section: "By degrees, the milky water of the agitated deep turned into clarified butter by virtue of those gums and juices. But nectar did not appear even then." (Ganguli, Adi Parva section 18)
candidates.story_plain: Long ago, the gods wanted amrita, a magic drink that lets you live forever. To get it, they had to churn the ocean, the way you churn milk into butter. A great snake pulled up Mount Mandara to be the churning stick. But the mountain needed something strong to stand on. So the gods asked the King of Tortoises, "Will you hold the mountain on your back?" The tortoise said yes, and the mountain was set on his back. The gods pulled one end of a long snake rope, the asuras pulled the other, and the mountain turned and turned. Little by little, the milky sea turned into butter, but still there was no amrita. The gods were so tired they wanted to stop, but they found new strength and churned again. At last wonderful things rose from the sea, and the healer of the gods came up holding a white pot of amrita.
candidates.link_to_theme: PARALLEL, and the best fit with a Primary series asana. Nobody moves the mountain in one go. The tortoise just holds it steady while everyone else works, and the change comes "by degrees". The gods even say "we are spent up", then start churning again, and the prize comes late. That is daily practice, with the teacher as the steady back underneath. FACTS BY VERSION. Who holds the mountain: in the Mahabharata it is "the king of tortoises". The Sanskrit (1.16.10) gives his name: "kūrmarājānam akūpāraṃ" (the tortoise king Akupara). The text never says he is Vishnu. The snake Ananta pulls up Mandara, and Indra presses it onto the tortoise's back (1.16.11). In the Vishnu Purana it is "Hari himself, in the form of a tortoise". In the Ramayana, Vishnu "The semblance of a tortoise wore" after the mountain sinks. In the Bhagavata (8.7.9), the Lord makes a huge tortoise body. In 5.18.30 the Bhagavata uses the name "akūpārāya" for Vishnu as the tortoise. How long they churned: the Mahabharata gives no number. Ganguli has "After the churning ... had gone on for some time", and the Sanskrit 1.16.29 says "cirārabdham" (begun long ago). The Ramayana says "a thousand seasons through" before the poison and "A thousand years had reached their close" before the healer rose. I found no number in the Vishnu Purana or Bhagavata passages. First and last: this changes from book to book. Mahabharata (Ganguli): the Moon comes first, then Lakshmi, Soma, the white horse, the Kaustubha jewel, Dhanvantari with the nectar, then Airavata, and "the poison Kalakuta appeared at last". (In the critical edition's notes, some manuscripts put a poison passage earlier.) Ramayana: poison first, "the Amrit" last. Vishnu Purana: the cow Surabhi first, the poison in the middle after the Moon, then Dhanvantari with the amrita, and Sri last. Bhagavata: Halahala poison first (8.7.19, "agrataḥ"), and Dhanvantari with a pot full of amrita last (8.8.31 to 35). So "poison first, amrita last" is only true for the Ramayana and the Bhagavata. BRIDGE TO THE ANCHOR: the same Liezi chapter 5 that tells of the Foolish Old Man also has giant turtles holding mountains: "乃命禺彊使巨鼇十五舉首而戴之。迭爲三番，六萬歲一交焉。五山始峙而不動。" My gloss: fifteen giant turtles lift their heads and carry the five mountains, taking turns in three shifts, changing once every 60,000 years, and then the mountains stood firm. Yu Gong's own story ends with two sons of Kua'e who "負二山", carry the two mountains on their backs. BEDTIME DETAIL (my gloss of the Sanskrit): in Bhagavata 8.7.11 and 2.7.13, the spinning mountain felt to the giant tortoise like someone scratching an itch on his back, and it made him sleepy.
candidates.practice_lesson: Be the tortoise, not the mountain. In Kurmasana, keep the breath slow and the base wide and steady, and let the stretch turn on top of you. In Supta Kurmasana, the shoulders slide a little further under the knees each day, by degrees, like milk turning into butter. When you feel "I am spent", do not force the bind. Breathe, rest, and come back tomorrow. The bind is the amrita, and it comes late.
candidates.safety_flags: Leave out the sea animals crushed by the mountain and the forest fire that burns lions and elephants (Ganguli section 18). Leave out the wine goddess (Sura, Varuni, Soma), Vishnu's enchantress form (Ganguli says she "coquetted" with the Danavas, which is adult in tone), Rahu's head being cut off, the eclipse, and the gods and asuras battle (section 19; the Ramayana calls it a "fratricidal war"). The poison and Shiva drinking it can stay only if told gently, or can be cut. Do not tell it as if the asuras were fools.

check.corrected_quote: The key quote is correct as given. Both parts are word for word in Ganguli, Section XVIII. Part 1: "The gods then went to the king of tortoises and said to him, 'O Tortoise-king, thou wilt have to hold the mountain on thy back!' The Tortoise-king agreed, and Indra contrived to place the mountain on the former's back." Part 2: "By degrees, the milky water of the agitated deep turned into clarified butter by virtue of those gums and juices. But nectar did not appear even then." Add these lines from the same section to support the "tired, then churn again" beat, so it is told honestly: "Sire, we are spent up, we have no strength left to churn further." and Narayana's reply: "Ye wise ones, I grant you sufficient strength. Go, put the mountain in position again and churn the water." and "Re-established thus in strength, the gods recommenced churning."
check.corrected_source: K. M. Ganguli (tr.), The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, Vol. 1, Adi Parva, Astika Parva, Section XVIII (published 1883 to 1896), Project Gutenberg eBook #15474. Sanskrit, critical edition (GRETIL): 1.16.10 "ūcuś ca kūrmarājānam akūpāraṃ surāsurāḥ / girer adhiṣṭhānam asya bhavān bhavitum arhati" and 1.16.11. Note: in the Sanskrit it is the gods AND the asuras (surāsurāḥ) who ask the tortoise, and they ask him to be the mountain's base (adhiṣṭhāna). 1.16.29 "cirārabdham idaṃ ... manthanam" and 1.16.30 to 31 (Vishnu: "balaṃ dadāmi", I give strength) confirmed. Other versions confirmed: Vishnu Purana Book I, Chapter IX, tr. H. H. Wilson 1840 (wisdomlib): "Hari himself, in the form of a tortoise, served as a pivot for the mountain"; Durvasas's curse opens the chapter. Griffith, Ramayan, Book I, Canto XLV "The Quest Of The Amrit" (Gutenberg #24869): "a thousand seasons through", "The semblance of a tortoise wore", "A thousand years had reached their close". check.asana_series_confirmed: Kurmasana: confirmed, Primary. In Yoga Mala (North Point Press English ed., checked in the archive.org OCR) the list has "22. KURMASANA", and the text says: "Kurmasana has sixteen vinyasas, the 7th and 9th vinyasas of which constitute the States of the asana. The State of the 9th vinyasa is called Supta Kurmasana [Reclined Tortoise]." The grimmly1997 Primary list (copied from ashtangadiary.com) also has Kurmasana and Supta Kurmasana. Yoga Mala says nothing about the churning, Mandara, Vishnu or any tortoise story. Kurma just means tortoise. So the honest wording is "the asana has the same name", never "named after this tortoise". Kasyapasana and Durvasasana: only from a secondary source. The grimmly1997 Advanced A list, which it credits to Matthew Sweeney's Astanga Yoga As It Is, spells them "Kashyapasana (or Kashyabasana)" and "Durvasana". Better text support for the Kashyapa hook than the claim's "all sons of Kashyapa" line: Griffith Ramayana I.45 says the rival gods and asuras "Were sons of Kaśyap lofty-souled", and Bhagavata 8.8.32 says the churners were "kāśyapair amṛtārthibhiḥ" (the sons of Kashyapa seeking amrita). Durvasa: Wilson's Vishnu Purana I.9 confirms that his curse starts that version. Again, these are same-name hooks only.
check.story_errors: 1) "they found new strength and churned again" is wrong. In Ganguli the gods go to Brahma and say "we are spent up". Brahma asks Narayana, and Narayana says "I grant you sufficient strength". So Vishnu GAVE them the strength. Say so. It is also a good match for Yu Gong, where heaven was "moved by his sincerity" (帝感其誠) and sent help. 2) "wanted to stop" is a small stretch. They said they had no strength left. They did not say they wanted to quit. 3) "the healer of the gods" is not in Ganguli, which just says "the divine Dhanwantari himself with the white vessel of nectar". Griffith calls him "Lord of the art of healing man". Use "Dhanvantari, the great healer". 4) "the mountain needed something strong to stand on" is not in Ganguli. The Sanskrit 1.16.10 does support it ("be the base of this mountain"), so it is OK if the Sanskrit is cited. 5) "At last ... amrita": in Ganguli, Airavata and then the Kalakuta poison come AFTER Dhanvantari, so amrita is not last in the version being quoted. It is fine for a bedtime cut, but do not say amrita was the very last thing in the Mahabharata. 6) Facts to fix in the claim's notes: (a) In the critical edition, the Kalakuta poison is not in the main text at all. It is only in extra manuscript passages, some early (appendix after 1.16.15 and 1.16.27) and some late (*0274 after 1.16.36). In the main text, Dhanvantari with the "white kamandalu" of amrita (1.16.37) is the last thing to rise. So "amrita last" is true of the critical-edition Mahabharata too, not only of the Ramayana and Bhagavata. (b) The "sleepy" detail is only in Bhagavata 2.7.13 (nidrākṣaṇaḥ) and 12.13.2 (nidrāloḥ). 8.7.11 has only the itch-scratching. (c) Dhanvantari is named at Bhagavata 8.8.36. (d) "I am spent" in the practice lesson is a paraphrase. If it goes on screen in quote marks, use "we are spent up". Correct as claimed: Ananta pulls up Mandara; Indra places it on the tortoise; Vasuki is the rope; asuras hold the hood and gods the tail; "By degrees" milk turns to clarified butter; no amrita yet; the white vessel; the Mahabharata never says the tortoise is Vishnu.
check.safety: Bedtime-safe if cut well. Leave out, as the claim says: sea creatures crushed and the forest fire burning lions and elephants (Section XVIII); the wine goddess (Sura, Varuni); Mohini who "coquetted with the Danavas"; Rahu's head cut off and the eclipse; the battle (Section XIX, and Griffith's "fratricidal war"). Shiva drinking the poison can stay only if told gently, or cut it. Also leave out: (1) The Liezi turtle passage goes on with a giant from Longbo who hooks six of the turtles and burns their bones, and two mountains sink with countless immortals lost. Stop the bridge at "五山始峙而不動" (the five mountains stood firm). (2) In Liezi, 帝 is the god of heaven. Say "the god of heaven", not "the emperor", so nothing sounds like human royalty. (3) "King of tortoises" is a myth animal, not human royalty, so the risk is low. To be extra safe, say "the great tortoise Akupara" in the voiceover. (4) Do not use the frame story of Sections XVI and XVII: Kadru and Vinata's bet, the slavery, and Garuda. Avoid Garuda images, because Garuda is the Thai royal emblem. Keep Vishnu only as a god. Do not link him to Thai kingship in any way. (5) Do not make the asuras look foolish. Bonus image, not a risk: Bhagavata 12.13.2 says the sleepy tortoise's breathing is why the tides still come and go and never rest. That fits breath and daily practice well, but it is my own gloss of the Sanskrit. No public-domain English quote was found.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The tortoise quote is real. I found it word for word in Ganguli's Mahabharata, Section 18, and the turtles holding mountains are in the same Liezi chapter as the Foolish Old Man. Fix two small things: Vishnu gave the tired gods their new strength, and Kurmasana only has the same name as this tortoise.

candidates.myth_title: Agastya and the Mountain That Kept Growing (Vindhya)
candidates.asana: None. No Ashtanga asana is named after Agastya. The nearest link is Nahusasana (Advanced B), named after Nahusha. The gods mention Nahusha's fall from heaven in the same Agastya passage, but it is a different story.
candidates.series_claim: There is no Agastyasana in Primary, Intermediate, Advanced A or Advanced B. I checked the four lists at grimmly1997.blogspot.com (from Ashtanga Diary and Matthew Sweeney) and the Primary list in Yoga Mala. Nahusasana A, B and C are on the Advanced B list on the same page.
candidates.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Tirtha-yatra Parva, sections CIII to CIV, tr. K. M. Ganguli (1883 to 1896), Project Gutenberg eBook 15474.
candidates.key_quote: "Until my return, do thou wait for me. And when I have returned, O king of mountains, thou mayst increase in bulk as much as thou pleasest." ... "up to the present day Varuna's son doth not return from the southern region." (Ganguli, Vana Parva section CIV)
candidates.story_plain: Every day, the Sun walked around Mount Meru, the golden mountain. Mount Vindhya felt jealous. "Walk around me too!" he said. The Sun said, "I cannot. This path was given to me." So Vindhya got angry and grew taller and taller, to block the Sun and the Moon. The gods begged him to stop, but he would not listen. So they asked the wise sage Agastya for help. Agastya came with his wife and said, "Please give me a path. I must go south. Wait for me until I come back, and then you may grow as much as you like." Vindhya agreed to wait. Agastya never came back from the south, so the mountain is still waiting and has not grown since.
candidates.link_to_theme: CONTRAST. This mountain tries to grow big fast, out of anger and envy of Meru, and a patient sage stops it with one quiet request. The Old Man's growth is the opposite: slow, and not about beating anyone. Keep it as a side note only, because the hero has no asana. NOTE: the popular detail that Vindhya "bowed down" is not in Ganguli's text. Agastya only asks for "a path", and Vindhya stops growing.
candidates.practice_lesson: There is no asana to teach with this one. If you use it at all: Vindhya grew because he envied the mountain next to him. Do not rush your practice because you envy the mat next to you.
candidates.safety_flags: The story itself is gentle. Leave out the surrounding text: Nahusha "thrown down from his throne of heaven" (royalty and pride), and the next part, where Agastya drinks the ocean so the gods can kill the Kalakeyas (violence). Tell Agastya kindly, not as a trickster: he only asked the mountain to wait for him.

check.corrected_quote: "O thou best of mountains! I wish to have a path given to me by thee, as, for some purpose, I shall have to go to the southern region. Until my return, do thou wait for me. And when I have returned, O king of mountains, thou mayst increase in bulk as much as thou pleasest." And, O slayer of foes! having made this compact with Vindhya up to the present day Varuna's son doth not return from the southern region. (Ganguli, Vana Parva, Section CIV. Both lines in the claim match the text word for word. The second line is cut off at its start, so it is better to give it with "having made this compact with Vindhya" in front.) Also note Section CIII, where the gods say of Vindhya: "But he hath ceased to increase, as he was unable to disobey thy command."
check.corrected_source: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, Book 3 Vana Parva, Tirtha-yatra Parva, Section CIV (the Vindhya story, told by Lomasa to Yudhishthira).
