check.asana_series_confirmed: Confirmed. No asana with Agastya in its name is on the Primary, Intermediate, Advanced A or Advanced B lists at grimmly1997.blogspot.com/p/asana-lists.html. The Primary and Intermediate lists come from Ashtanga Diary. The Advanced A and B lists come from Matthew Sweeney's "Astanga Yoga As It Is". It is also not on the Advanced C/D list on that page. "Nahusasana A B C" is on the Advanced B list, second after Mula Bandhasana. I did not open Yoga Mala myself. The claim says Nahusasana is "named after Nahusha". No source I opened says that. The honest wording is "Nahusasana has the same name as King Nahusha". Nahusha is a fallen king of heaven, so he also breaks the no-royalty rule. Do not use him as the asana link.
check.story_errors: Mostly faithful. These parts are added or stretched: (1) "Mount Vindhya felt jealous." The text never says jealous or envy. It says "wrath" and "made senseless with wrath". Section CIII calls it "a wrathful competition with the sun (i. e., to rival him in altitude)". So the rival there is the Sun, not Meru. Better: "Vindhya wanted that honor too, and he got angry." The "envy of Meru" in link_to_theme is also a guess, not the text. (2) "I cannot." The Sun really says "I do not of my own will honour this mountain... By those who have built this universe hath that path been assigned to me." Better: "I did not choose this path. The makers of the world gave it to me." (3) "The gods begged him." The text says the gods "tried to dissuade him", and "he heeded not". Better: "tried to talk him out of it." (4) "The mountain is still waiting." This is a fair guess, but the text only says Agastya "doth not return" and Vindhya "doth not increase in bulk". (5) "Grew taller and taller" leaves out "suddenly". The text says he "suddenly began to increase". Keep "suddenly", because it is the heart of the contrast with slow daily work. (6) In link_to_theme and safety_flags, "one quiet request" and "he only asked" are only half the picture. In Section CIV, Agastya asks for a path. But in Section CIII the gods call it his "command" ("unable to disobey thy command"), and they say Vindhya stopped "by reason of the power of Agastya". The claim is right that "bowed down" is not in Ganguli. The details that are in the text: the Sun goes round golden Meru every day, Vindhya asks for the same, the gods go to Agastya, Agastya comes with his wife, he asks for a path south and tells Vindhya to wait, and he never comes back.
check.safety: The Vindhya story on its own (Section CIV, first half) is gentle and fine for bedtime. The text around it is not. Leave it all out. Section CII, just before, is very violent: the Kalakeyas eat sages at night, and there are bodies "without flesh and without blood" and "heaps of bones". Section CIII has Vritra being killed, and Nahusha "thrown down from his throne of heaven" (royalty and a fall from a throne). It also says "the born beings were harassed by death" in the darkness. The second half of Section CIV and Section CV have Agastya drinking the ocean "full of wrath", and then the gods kill the demons (war and violence). "King of mountains" is only a name for a mountain, but you can say "great mountain" to stay far from royalty words. Tell Agastya with respect. Do not make him a trickster or make fun of him. Say he went south and stayed there. No Thai royal link and no politics.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The quote is real. I found it word for word in Ganguli's Mahabharata, Vana Parva, section 104. But no Ashtanga asana is named for Agastya, so this story cannot lead a Reel in your series. Use it only as a short side note: Vindhya grew suddenly out of anger, and the Old Man moved his mountain slowly, one basket a day.

candidates.myth_title: The Small Boy Who Asked for Three Steps (Vamana becomes Trivikrama)
candidates.asana: Trivikramasana and Supta Trivikramasana. Extra hook: Kasyapasana, because Vamana is "the son of Kasyapa by Aditi" (Vishnu Purana 3.1).
candidates.series_claim: Advanced A. On the Advanced A list at grimmly1997.blogspot.com (from Matthew Sweeney's Astanga Yoga As It Is), Supta Trivikramasana comes right after Hanumanasana, and Trivikramasana comes after Digasana. This repo's ashtanga-graph.js also has both as 'Advance A'. Both are secondary sources.
candidates.source: Rig Veda 1.154.1 to 3, tr. R. T. H. Griffith (2nd ed. 1896). I opened it on the rigveda-online mirror because sacred-texts.com blocked me. Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda Canto XXXI 'The Perfect Hermitage', tr. Griffith (1870 to 1874), Gutenberg eBook 24869. Vishnu Purana 3.1, tr. H. H. Wilson (1840), on wisdomlib (Wilson's note says the Vishnu Purana has no fuller account). Bhagavata Purana 8.19.16 to 19, Sanskrit only (GRETIL), with my own gloss.
candidates.key_quote: "The God a dwarflike shape indued: / Before Virochan's son he came, / Three steps of land his only claim." (Griffith, Ramayana Book I, Canto XXXI, footnote number removed). And the mountain link from Rig Veda 1.154.3 (Griffith): "Let the hymn lift itself as strength to Viṣṇu, the Bull far-striding, dwelling on the mountains, Him who alone with triple step hath measured this common dwelling-place, long, far extended."
candidates.story_plain: Long ago, a strong asura named Bali took over all three worlds, and the gods were afraid. They asked Vishnu for help. Vishnu came to Bali as a tiny boy, a dwarf named Vamana. He asked for one small gift: "Just three steps of land, measured by my own feet." Bali said, "You are only a boy. That is a silly wish!" But the boy wanted only three steps, and Bali said yes. Then the boy grew and grew until he was huge. With his first step he covered the whole earth, and with his second, the sky. With his third step he went right through heaven.
candidates.link_to_theme: MIXED. PARALLEL: the small one asks for something tiny and gets called foolish, just like the Wise Old Man of the River Bend laughing at Yu Gong. In Bhagavata 8.19.18, Bali says "tvaṃ bālo bāliśamatiḥ" (my gloss: you are a boy with a childish mind), and in 8.19.19 he calls the one who picks three steps "abuddhimān" (not wise). The Ramayana also says that, before he became the dwarf, Vishnu lived at that grove "For holy thought and rites austere / Of penance", so practice came first. The Rig Veda gives the mountain link: "dwelling on the mountains" and "mountain-roaming" (1.154.2 to 3). CONTRAST: the three steps are not small steps. He grows huge in a moment. Be honest about this if you use it.
candidates.practice_lesson: Three small asks. Start lying down in Supta Trivikramasana and ask the leg for just a little more each week. Later, stand up into Trivikramasana. Small requests, kept up every day, turn into the big stride. Keep the standing leg straight and the hips level, and never yank the leg with the arm.
candidates.safety_flags: Bali is a ruler: Griffith calls him "that demon king" with an "empire" over the three worlds. That touches the no royalty rule, so call him "a strong asura named Bali" and do not stress kingship. Leave out the ending: in the Ramayana Bali is "hurled / By Vishṇu to the nether world", and in the Bhagavata (8.21) he is bound. End the story at the three steps. Do not mock Bali (the Bhagavata honours him), and do not make Vamana a sneaky trickster.

check.corrected_quote:
Both quotes match word for word. Use the source's own spelling and apostrophes:
(1) Griffith, Ramayan, Book I, Canto XXXI: "The God a dwarflike shape indued: / Before Virochan’s son he came, / Three steps of land his only claim." (footnote mark (168) removed). The next lines, also verified: "The whole broad earth from side to side / He measured with one mighty stride, / Spanned with the next the firmament, / And with the third through heaven he went."
(2) Griffith, Rig Veda 1.154.3: "Let the hymn lift itself as strength to Viṣṇu, the Bull far-striding, dwelling on the mountains, Him who alone with triple step hath measured this common dwelling-place, long, far extended." 1.154.2 really does have "mountain-roaming", but in the line "like some wild beast, dread, prowling, mountain-roaming". That simile is not good for a bedtime story.
(3) Vishnu Purana 3.1 (Wilson): "Viṣṇu was again born as Vāmana, the son of Kaśyapa by Aditī. With three paces he subdued the worlds, and gave them, freed from all embarrassment, to Purandara."
(4) A new line you could use. Griffith's own note 169 on this canto says: "This is a solar allegory. Vishṇu is the sun, the three steps being his rising, culmination, and setting." This is the translator's opinion. It is not the Ramayana's text.
The lines spoken by the characters in story_plain are not quotes from any translation (see story_errors).
check.corrected_source:
Valmiki Ramayana, Book I (Bala Kanda), Canto XXXI "The Perfect Hermitage", verse translation by Ralph T. H. Griffith (1870 to 1874), Project Gutenberg eBook #24869 (re-downloaded and checked line by line). In note 167, at this exact spot, Griffith says he leaves out eight slokas, so his verse is not a full translation. The canto is spoken by Vishvamitra.
Rig Veda 1.154.1 to 3, tr. R. T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda (1896; Wikisource gives the year as 1896). Checked on the rigveda-online mirror and again on en.wikisource. The text is identical except Wikisource writes "Visnu". sacred-texts.com is still behind a Cloudflare challenge.
Vishnu Purana Book 3, Chapter 1, tr. H. H. Wilson (1840), wisdomlib. Wilson's note 22 says "There is no further account of this incarnation in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa. Fuller details occur in the Bhāgavata, Kūrma, Matsya, and Vāmana Purāṇas."
Bhagavata Purana 8.19.16 to 20, 8.19.28 and 8.19.32, Sanskrit only (GRETIL plaintext). No published English translation was opened, so every English line from the Bhagavata is the researcher's own gloss and must be labelled that way.
checked_urls: https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/太平御覽/0040 (search result snippet quoting Liezi: 河曲智叟笑而止之曰：甚矣，汝之不慧)
check.asana_series_confirmed: Yes, both are in Advanced A (Third Series). ashtangayoga.info (Ronald Steiner) gives the order Hanumanasana, Supta Trivikramasana, Digasana A, Digasana B, Utthita Trivikramasana, Natarajasana. That page calls the standing one "Utthita Trivikramasana". Kasyapasana is also in Advanced A, third in the series after Vasisthasana and Visvamitrasana. The repo's ashtanga-graph.js lines 171 to 174 agree. I did not open the grimmly blog. On the name: Trivikrama ("three steps") is Vishnu's title in this story, so honest wording is "the same name". The nearest claim found is Steiner's page, which only says the asana "recalls Trivikrama's mythic great step". No source says the asana was named after the story. Kasyapasana only has the same name as Vamana's father (Kashyapa). Vishnu Purana 3.1 and Bhagavata 8.19.30 ("kaśyapād aditer jātaḥ") back that up. Kasyapasana is named for the sage, not for this story, so it is a weak hook.
check.story_errors:
1) Neither line in quote marks comes from a translation. "Just three steps of land, measured by my own feet" is the researcher's gloss of Bhagavata 8.19.16, which asks for "mahīm īṣat", a little land: three steps measured by my FOOT ("padā", singular). It is fine as storytelling, but it must not go on screen as a quote.
2) "You are only a boy. That is a silly wish!" makes Bali sound unkind, and the source does not. In 8.19.18 Bali first praises the boy ("your words are approved by elders") and then says "tvaṃ bālo bāliśamatiḥ svārthaṃ praty abudhaḥ": a boy with a childish mind who does not see his own good. His complaint is that the boy asks for TOO LITTLE. In 8.19.20 Bali offers enough land to live on. In 8.19.28 he laughs and says "take what you wish". The story leaves out this generosity. The Ramayana also says of Bali: "The suit of none is e'er denied."
3) It mixes two versions. The boy and Bali's words come from the Bhagavata. The ending (earth, then sky, then "through heaven") comes from Griffith's Ramayana. In the Bhagavata the third step has nowhere to go (8.19.34). Pick one version or say it is a blend.
4) "Grew and grew" is close enough, but the growth is sudden ("in wondrous wise"), not gradual.
5) link_to_theme: the parallel with the Wise Old Man is real, and stronger than the claim says. Bali also LAUGHS (8.19.28 "hasann āha") and calls the asker "abuddhimān". The Liezi (as quoted in the Taiping Yulan, juan 40) has 河曲智叟笑而止之曰：甚矣，汝之不慧. But the direction is reversed. Yu Gong is mocked for trying too much with too little. Vamana is mocked for asking too little.
6) The Bhagavata's own lesson here (8.19.21 to 27) is contentment: a person not happy with three steps will not be filled even by a whole continent. That is not persistence.
7) "Before he became the dwarf, Vishnu lived at that grove" is loosely supported. The text has Vishnu's penance there, and the gods "Sought Vishṇu in this place of rest" and then asked for the dwarfish form. "Practice came first" is the researcher's reading, not something the text says.
check.safety:
FAILS the no-royalty and no-politics rules, so drop for this Reel.
(a) Royalty is the whole plot, not one word in it. Bali is a king in every source: Ramayana "that demon king" and "O'er the three worlds his empire held"; Bhagavata "rājan" (8.19.17), "daityendra" (8.19.16), "lokānām ekam īśvaram" (8.19.19). The story is about who rules the three worlds, and it ends with the universe "restored / To Indra’s rule". Calling him "a strong asura" changes the word but leaves the plot.
(b) Live politics and caste. In Kerala the Vamana and Mahabali story is the Onam myth and a real political fight. On 13 Sep 2016 Amit Shah posted "Vamana Jayanti" wishes. Kerala CM Pinarayi Vijayan said: "By eulogising Vamana and denigrating Mahabali, BJP national president Amit Shah has humiliated Kerala and our festival Onam" (The News Minute). Search results show the debate is still going in Aug 2026 (an Organiser article, which I saw only as a search result). A Reel that cheers the boy and quietly drops Bali can be read as taking a side.
(c) Trick and blame. The sources themselves call the dwarf form illusion: Ramayana "with thine own illusive art"; Bhagavata 8.19.32 has Shukra call him "māyā-māṇavakaḥ", a boy by illusion. In Bhagavata 8.15.2 the narrator even asks why the blameless ("anāgasaḥ") Bali was bound. A generous giver losing everything to a disguised asker is hard to tell to children without it sounding like a trick by a god, which goes against "never mock a god".
(d) Violence to cut. Ramayana: Bali "hurled / By Vishṇu to the nether world". Bhagavata 8.21.26: Garuda binds him with Varuna's ropes. The setting is Bali's march on heaven (8.15). Ending at the third step leaves the story unfinished.
(e) Small fixes if it is ever reused: say "a very small boy", not "dwarf", and skip the "wild beast, dread, prowling" simile in Rig Veda 1.154.2.
(f) Practice: Supta Trivikramasana and Trivikramasana are Advanced A asanas. The lesson should say they are only for students whose teacher has given them these asanas, because forcing them risks the hamstrings, the adductors and the hips.
A safer future angle is the Rig Veda alone (Vishnu's three strides measure the world, with no Bali and no king), plus Griffith's note that the three steps are the sun rising, at its highest, and setting every day. That is safe but thin, and it loses the "laughed at" parallel.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The quotes are real and the two Trivikramasana asanas are really in Advanced A. But this story is about a king losing his worlds, and in Kerala it is a hot political fight, so it breaks our safety rules. Also the boy's three steps are huge and happen in one moment, not small steps every day, so I would drop it for this Reel.

candidates.asana: None. No Ashtanga asana is named after Krishna or Govardhana.
candidates.series_claim: No such asana is in Primary, Intermediate, Advanced A or Advanced B. I checked the lists at grimmly1997.blogspot.com and the Yoga Mala Primary list.
candidates.source: Vishnu Purana, Book V, Chapter XI, tr. H. H. Wilson (1840), on wisdomlib. Also Bhagavata Purana 2.7.32, Sanskrit (GRETIL), which also gives seven days and one hand.
candidates.key_quote: "Kṛṣṇa immediately plucked up the mountain Govarddhana, and held it aloft with one hand in sport" ... "For seven days and nights did the vast clouds sent by Indra rain upon the Gokula of Nanda to destroy its inhabitants, but they were protected by the elevation of the mountain" (Wilson, Vishnu Purana 5.11)
candidates.story_plain: That year, the cowherd people of Vraja did not hold their festival for Indra, the god of rain. Indra was upset and sent huge dark clouds full of rain. Krishna wanted to keep his friends and their cows safe. He pulled up Govardhana hill and held it high with one hand, like a big umbrella. "Come under the mountain," he said. "You will be safe here." Everyone came under it with their cows, out of the rain. Krishna held the mountain steady over their heads. For seven days and seven nights the rain fell, and then Indra told the clouds to stop.
candidates.link_to_theme: CONTRAST. He lifts it with one hand, all at once, "in sport". The one honest link is steadiness: Wilson says the mountain was one "which Kṛṣṇa held steadily over their heads" for seven days. But there is no asana, so it cannot carry an episode of this series.
candidates.practice_lesson: There is no asana to teach with this one. If you use it as a side note: in any long hold, the work is to stay steady and keep the breath smooth, not to look strong.
candidates.safety_flags: Indra sends the storm "to destroy its inhabitants", which is close to the no disasters rule. There is also a risk of showing Indra badly, which breaks the never mock a god rule. Keep Indra respectful if you use it at all.

check.corrected_quote: Quotes are correct as given. Both lines are in Wilson's Vishnu Purana, Book V, Chapter XI, exactly as written: "Kṛṣṇa immediately plucked up the mountain Govarddhana, and held it aloft with one hand in sport" and "For seven days and nights did the vast clouds sent by Indra rain upon the Gokula of Nanda to destroy its inhabitants, but they were protected by the elevation of the mountain". Also exact: "which Kṛṣṇa held steadily over their heads". A useful extra line from the same paragraph, word for word: "I will lift up this spacious mountain from its stony base, and hold it up, as a large umbrella, over the cow-pens." Krishna's real words to the people are: "Lo the mountain is on high; enter beneath it quickly, and it will shelter you from the storm: here you will be secure and at your ease in places defended from the wind: enter without delay, and fear not that the mountain will fall."
check.corrected_source: Vishnu Purana, Book V, Chapter XI ("Anger of Indra and holding Govardhana mountain by Krishna"), tr. H. H. Wilson (1840), wisdomlib. The festival set-up is in Book V, Chapter X. Bhagavata Purana 2.7.32 (Sanskrit, GRETIL bhp_02u.htm) is confirmed: "dhartocchilīndhram iva saptadināni sapta / varṣo mahīdhram anaghaikakare salīlam" (seven days, one hand, in play, Krishna aged seven, holding the mountain like a mushroom). No English translation of 2.7.32 was opened, so any English wording for it must be our own gloss and must not go in quotation marks.
checked_urls: https://www.ashtangayoga.info/ashtanga-yoga/3rd-series-sthira-bhaga/ (a local copy saved earlier in this workflow, plus the ashtangayoga.info Primary, Intermediate and Advanced A PDFs and series pages, all searched for Krishna or Govardhana)
check.asana_series_confirmed: The claim is correct. No asana is named after Krishna or Govardhana. I checked the ashtangayoga.info lists and PDFs for Primary, Intermediate and Advanced A, and the grimmly1997 asana-lists page for Advanced B (taken from Matthew Sweeney) and Advanced C and D. Krishna and Govardhana appear in none of them. Supta and Utthita Trivikramasana name Trivikrama (Vishnu's Vamana form), not Krishna, so they are not an honest link. Parvatasana ("mountain") appears only in the old Advanced C/D list from Swenson's DVD. It has no tie to Govardhana. I did not open Yoga Mala myself, so the claim's "Yoga Mala Primary list" check is unverified, but the result is the same. With no asana, this story cannot fill the "myth, then asana" slot of the Hidden Stories series.
check.story_errors: 1) "That year" is not in the source. Wilson Ch. X says "At this season" (autumn). 2) An important part is left out. In Ch. X it is Krishna himself who talks the cowherds out of Indra's sacrifice. He tells them to worship Govardhana and the cows instead, and Wilson says he "determined to put the king of the celestials into a passion". Saying the people just "did not hold their festival" hides why Indra was angry. 3) The quote "Come under the mountain. You will be safe here." is a paraphrase written as if it were his real words. Use Wilson's real words or drop the quotation marks. 4) Smaller softenings that are fine for a bedtime story but are not the source's words: "upset" (source: "exceedingly angry") and "huge dark clouds full of rain" (source: the Samvarttaka clouds, a "fearful storm of rain and wind, to destroy the cattle"). 5) Everything else is supported: one hand, "as a large umbrella", the people and herds sheltering, held "steadily over their heads", seven days and nights, Indra "commanded the clouds to cease". Not an error but left out: Krishna puts the mountain back at the end.
check.safety: Risky for a bedtime Reel. (a) Disaster: the source storm is sent "to destroy" the cattle and the people, cattle "gave up their breath", and calves are "carried away by the flood". All of this must be cut, and even a softened flood is close to the no-disasters rule. (b) God conflict: Krishna sets out to anger Indra, and Indra is "foiled". This easily reads as one god beating another, so it risks mocking Indra. Keep Indra respectful or leave him out. (c) Chapter X asks the people to "kill a victim in due form" (an animal sacrifice). Leave it out. (d) Nanda's speech mentions "sovereign princes" offering to Indra, and Indra is called "king of the celestials". Avoid the king wording to stay clear of the royalty rule. (e) Do not pull lines from the next verse, Bhagavata 2.7.33. It is the rasa dance and has adult content. (f) Wilson's note says Shishupala mocked the hill as "an ant hill". Do not use it. (g) Contrast danger: a line like "Krishna did it the easy way, you have to do it the hard way" could read as making light of a living deity. Any contrast line must honour Krishna.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The quotes are real, word for word, from Wilson's 1840 Vishnu Purana. But no Ashtanga asana has this name. Krishna lifts the hill all at once with one hand, which is the opposite of the old man's basket a day. Do not use it as this Reel's story. If you use it at all, keep it to one kind line about holding steady, and keep Indra respectful.

candidates.myth_title: Manu and the Little Fish That Grew (Matsya)
candidates.asana: Matsyasana. Optional second hook: Navasana, the boat.
candidates.series_claim: Primary, finishing part. In K. Pattabhi Jois's Yoga Mala, Matsyasana is no. 37 on the Primary list (with the finishing asanas), and Navasana is no. 20. Matsyasana is also on the Primary finishing list at grimmly1997.blogspot.com (from Ashtanga Diary).
candidates.source: Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1.1 to 6, tr. Julius Eggeling, Sacred Books of the East vol. 12 (1882), on wisdomlib. I also read a printed SBE 12 text copy. Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya Parva, section CLXXXVI, tr. K. M. Ganguli, Project Gutenberg eBook 15474.
candidates.key_quote: "Thou wilt first keep me in a jar. When I outgrow that, thou wilt dig a pit and keep me in it. When I outgrow that, thou wilt take me down to the sea, for then I shall be beyond destruction." ... "As the water subsides, thou mayest gradually descend!' Accordingly he gradually descended" (Eggeling, Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1.3 and 1.8.1.6)
candidates.story_plain: One morning, the wise man Manu was washing his hands, and a tiny fish swam into them. "Please look after me," said the fish. "While I am small, big fish eat little fish. One day I will save you." So Manu kept the fish in a jar. When it grew too big for the jar, he dug a pond for it. When it grew too big for the pond, he carried it down to the sea. Bit by bit, with Manu's care, the little fish had become a giant fish. Later the fish kept its promise and pulled Manu's boat all the way up to a high northern mountain. "Now go down slowly," said the fish. And Manu walked down the mountain, little by little.
candidates.link_to_theme: PARALLEL, and the best new fit for "big things come from small things done every day". Growth here is slow and needs daily care. Ganguli says Manu "tended it carefully like a child". The carer moves the fish to a bigger home only when it outgrows the old one: jar, then pond, then sea. That is how an Ashtanga teacher gives the next asana. There is a mountain at both ends: the fish pulls the boat up the mountain, and Manu comes down "gradually". In the Mahabharata the boat is tied to "the highest peak of the Himavat", called Naubandhana, and the fish "diligently dragged the boat ... for many a long year". In the Mahabharata the fish says "I am Brahma", not Vishnu as in later Puranas. It pairs well with Yu Gong: small acts, kept up, outgrow the impossible. Your unfilmed Bharadvaja (three mountains) script is still the closest twin to Yu Gong, but this is the best new story. WORDING NOTE: wisdomlib names the slope "Alarm's descent", while the printed SBE 12 copy I read says "Manu's descent". It looks like a scanning error, so do not quote that name.
candidates.practice_lesson: Matsyasana comes near the very end of the Primary series, after many other asanas, just as the fish reaches the sea last. In the asana, lift the chest a little more each day and keep the weight in the elbows, not hanging on the neck. Like the fish, you get a bigger home only when you have outgrown the small one.
candidates.safety_flags: The great flood is a disaster, and the rule is no disasters. The Shatapatha says "The flood then swept away all these creatures, and Manu alone remained here", and Ganguli speaks of the world's "dissolution" and a "fearful flood". Leave all of that out. Either end the story with the fish safe in the sea, or say only that the fish pulled Manu's boat up a mountain, without naming the flood. Ganguli's line that the boat "reeled about like a drunken harlot" is adult and must be cut. Use the Shatapatha or Mahabharata Manu (a sage), not the Bhagavata, where he is King Satyavrata, because of the royalty rule.

check.corrected_quote: Use the jar quote. It is word for word, but trim it to 1.8.1.3 only: "As long as we are small, there is great destruction for us: fish devours fish. Thou wilt first keep me in a jar. When I outgrow that, thou wilt dig a pit and keep me in it. When I outgrow that, thou wilt take me down to the sea, for then I shall be beyond destruction." (Eggeling, Shatapatha Brahmana 1.8.1.3). Leave out the 1.8.1.6 line ("As the water subsides, thou mayest gradually descend!' Accordingly he gradually descended"). It is word for word too, but "the water" there is the flood, so it cannot be used once the flood is cut. For the slow, caring growth, quote Ganguli instead. These lines are word for word in Mahabharata Vana Parva section CLXXXVI: "Manu tended it carefully like a child." / "Worshipful sir, do thou appoint some better habitation for me." / "as I have grown to this great bulk by thy favour".

I checked it against the printed scan at archive.org/details/wg912 (djvu text) and against wisdomlib doc63144. check.asana_series_confirmed: Partly confirmed. Matsyasana belongs to the finishing (closing) asanas. It comes after Sarvangasana, Halasana, Karnapidasana, Urdhva Padmasana and Pindasana, and is done at the end of Primary and of every other series. It is not one of the Primary seated asanas. The practice_lesson should say "in the finishing asanas at the end of practice", not "near the very end of the Primary series". Yoga Mala does count the finishing asanas in its 42-asana list. Web search summaries give Matsyasana as no. 37 and Navasana as no. 20, but I could not open Yoga Mala myself: the archive.org copy is restricted, so treat those numbers as secondary. Wikipedia, citing Maehle 2007, p. 120, places Matsyasana in the Primary Series as the counterpose to Sarvangasana. Navasana is a Primary seated asana. Name link: "matsya" just means "fish". Wikipedia gives the Gheranda Samhita 2.21 (17th c.) as the earliest text naming the asana. No source I opened says Matsyasana was named after Manu's fish, and the Shatapatha does not even call the fish Matsya or a god. Use "the same name" or "the fish asana". The fish is Brahma in the Mahabharata, so do not call it Vishnu when citing these two sources. The Navasana "boat" hook only works through the flood boat, so drop it.
check.story_errors: 1) "Bit by bit... had become a giant fish": the Shatapatha says the opposite. Eggeling has "It soon became a jhasha (a large fish)", and his footnote 3 gives Muir's "Straightway he became a large fish". Slow growth is only in the Mahabharata ("after a long while", "the fish grew for many a long year"). The story quietly mixes two sources. 2) "jar, pond, sea" is the Shatapatha order, where it is a "pit" you dig, not a pond. The Mahabharata has four homes: an earthen water-vessel, a large tank two yojanas long, the river Ganga, then the sea. The link_to_theme cites Ganguli's care lines next to the Shatapatha's three homes as if they were one text. 3) "washing his hands": the source says water was brought "for washing" and "When he was washing himself, a fish came into his hands". This is minor. 4) "One day I will save you" and the boat on the mountain both depend on the flood ("A flood will carry away all these creatures"). Once the flood is cut, a boat going up a mountain makes no sense to a child, and the promise is left hanging. 5) The Shatapatha says the boat "passed swiftly up to yonder northern mountain". That is fast, not slow. 6) "Now go down slowly": in the source the reason is "As the water subsides... let not the water cut thee off". It is about flood water going down, not patience or practice. "Walked" is added. 7) link_to_theme says "a mountain at both ends". Both ends need the flood, so the mountain parallel to Yu Gong does not survive the safety cut. SAFE FIX (Shatapatha plus one Ganguli line): One morning, a wise man named Manu was washing. A tiny fish came into his hands. "Please look after me," it said. "While we are small, big fish eat little fish." So Manu kept the fish in a jar. When it grew too big, he dug a pit with water for it. He cared for it like a child. When it grew too big again, he carried it down to the sea. Now the fish was big and safe. End there.
check.safety: The flood is the heart of this myth, and the "no disasters" rule rules it out. Eggeling's chapter is the deluge legend: "The flood then swept away all these creatures, and Manu alone remained here." Ganguli has "dissolution", "the terrible doom", "fearful flood" and "cataclysm". The whole back half has to go: the promise to save him, the ship, the horn and rope, the mountain and Naubandhana. Navasana goes too. Cut Ganguli's "the vessel reeled about like a drunken harlot" (adult). Stop the Shatapatha at 1.8.1.5. From 1.8.1.7 on, a woman is born from offerings and "Mitra and Varuna... desired to have a share in her", which does not suit a bedtime story. "Fish devours fish" is mild and fine for children. Royalty: the Mahabharata Manu is called a Rishi, but Ganguli also calls him "that lord of men" and "the conqueror of hostile cities", which are royal and war words. In later tradition Vaivasvata Manu is the first king and father of the solar line, and the Bhagavata makes him King Satyavrata. So use the Shatapatha wording: "a wise man named Manu". Never call him king. Nothing here mocks a god or sage, and it is safe once trimmed.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The quotes are real and word for word. The big part of this myth is a flood, so tell only the first half: jar, then pit, then sea. Then Manu is like a teacher who moves a student to the next asana only when they are ready, but no mountain moves, so it backs up Yu Gong rather than replacing him.

candidates.myth_title: Four Generations Bring the Ganga Down the Mountain (Kapila and Bhagiratha)
candidates.asana: Kapilasana. This is a weak link: Kapila is the sage in the story, not the one who keeps trying.
candidates.series_claim: Advanced B. It is on the Advanced B list at grimmly1997.blogspot.com (from Matthew Sweeney's Astanga Yoga As It Is). That is a secondary source, and Advanced B lists differ between sources.
candidates.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, Cantos XL to XLIV ('The Cleaving of the Earth', 'Kapil', 'Sagar's Sacrifice', 'Bhagírath', 'The Descent of Gangá'), tr. R. T. H. Griffith (1870 to 1874), Project Gutenberg eBook 24869.
candidates.key_quote: "Thus thirty thousand years he spent, / And then to heaven the monarch went." ... "There on his fruitless hope intent / Twice sixteen thousand years he spent" ... "The fervent king a year remained / With arms upraised, refusing rest / While with one toe the earth he pressed" (Griffith, Book I, Cantos XLII to XLIV)
candidates.story_plain: Long ago, sixty thousand brothers dug deep under the earth, looking for a lost horse. They found it next to the great sage Kapila, and they shouted at him in anger. Kapila's power turned them all to ash. Only the holy river Ganga, flowing in heaven, could wash the ashes clean and set them free. First old Sagar tried all his life to bring the river down, but he could not. Then his grandson Anshuman tried all his life, but he could not. Then Anshuman's son Dilipa tried, but he could not either. Then Dilipa's son Bhagiratha kept going, and he even stood for a whole year with his arms up, on one toe. At last Shiva stood on top of the snowy mountain and caught the river on his head. So the Ganga came down to earth, because the family never gave up.
candidates.link_to_theme: PARALLEL. This is the closest Indian echo of Yu Gong's "my sons and grandsons will keep going": four generations try, and the last one succeeds. The mountain link is that Ganga is the "daughter of the Lord of Snow", and Shiva catches her standing "upon the lofty crest / That crowns the Lord of Snow". The weak point is that the asana's namesake, Kapila, is not the hero of the long effort. His anger is what starts the trouble.
candidates.practice_lesson: Kapilasana is in Advanced B, and almost no student will ever practice it. So use the lesson, not the asana: some work takes longer than one try or one teacher. Keep going, and pass it on.
candidates.safety_flags: Heavy flags. Sagar, Anshuman, Dilipa and Bhagiratha are all kings, which breaks the no royalty rule. The sixty thousand sons dig in anger and "Innumerable creatures die". Kapila burns them "to heaps of ashes". The reason for the river is to wash the dead. Indra steals the horse in disguise, which risks showing a god badly. My advice is not to use this for a bedtime story. If you must, use only Bhagiratha's patience, but then the asana link is lost.

check.corrected_quote: All three quotes match the text word for word. Canto XLII (Sagar): "Thus thirty thousand years he spent, / And then to heaven the monarch went." Canto XLIII (Anshuman): "There on his fruitless hope intent / Twice sixteen thousand years he spent," Canto XLIV (Bhagiratha): "The fervent king a year remained / With arms upraised, refusing rest / While with one toe the earth he pressed," Two lines from the same canto fit the theme better if this story is ever used. (a) After the river gets lost in Shiva's hair: "Bhagírath saw it, and anew / His penance dire began." (b) Brahma's summing up: "Then Anśumán, dear Prince! although / No brighter name the world could show, / Strove long the heavenly flood to gain / To visit earth, but strove in vain." (Canto XLIV)
check.corrected_source: Valmiki, The Rámáyan of Válmíki, translated into English verse by Ralph T. H. Griffith (London: Trübner & Co.; Benares: E. J. Lazarus and Co., 1870-1874). Book I, Canto XL "The Cleaving Of The Earth", XLI "Kapil", XLII "Sagar's Sacrifice", XLIII "Bhagírath", XLIV "The Descent Of Gangá". Project Gutenberg eBook #24869 (plain text at gutenberg.org/cache/epub/24869/pg24869.txt). The claim's citation is correct.
check.asana_series_confirmed: Partly confirmed, from secondary sources only. Kapilasana is on the Advanced B list at grimmly1997.blogspot.com/p/asana-lists.html, which says "The list was taken from Matthew Sweeney's Astanga Yoga As It Is book", in this order: Mula Bandhasana, Nahusasana, Vrshchikasana A, Shayanasana, Buddhasana, Kapilasana, and so on. The same page also has it in the "Original" 1974 Advanced syllabus that Pattabhi Jois gave Nancy Gilgoff and David Williams, listed after Buddhasana. Krishnamacharya's asana list on the Yogasanagalu translation page also has it. I did not open a KPJAYI or Sharath primary source. Name link: wisdomlib only says Kapilasana is "Kapila (name of a ṛṣi)" plus asana. No source I found says the asana is named after the Kapila of the Sagar story. In Griffith that Kapil is Vishnu "In Kapil's form he loved to wear" (Canto XLI; footnotes 185 and 190 say "Vishṇu"). Harmony Slater's blog tells the Sagara story next to Kapilasana, but it never says the asana was named for it. Honest wording is "the same name".
check.story_errors: 1) "looking for a lost horse": the horse was stolen. Indra, "Veiling his form in demon guise", drove it away (Canto XL). "Lost" softens this. It is fine for a bedtime version, but it is not what the source says. 2) "they shouted at him in anger": the source has them rush at him: "on him rushed the furious band / Crying aloud, Stand, villain! stand!" (Canto XLI). 3) "the great sage Kapila": in this translation he is Vasudeva (Vishnu) in Kapil's form, called "the everlasting God". He is not only a sage. 4) "First old Sagar tried all his life": Canto XLII says he "longed" and "pondered long" but "found no plan". He thought about it and never found a way to try. Brahma later says he "mourned the boon he sought denied". 5) "Dilipa tried": Canto XLIII only says he pondered and "no cure could find". Only Brahma's speech in Canto XLIV says he sought it "with fierce prayers". 6) Bhagiratha: the story skips his first "Thousands of years" of penance among five fires, which won Brahma's boon. The year on one toe came after that, to win Shiva. It also skips the best theme beat: the river wandered in Shiva's hair "many lengthening seasons", and Bhagiratha began his penance "anew". 7) "because the family never gave up" is the writer's own moral. Brahma credits Bhagiratha alone: "But thou, O King, earned success". The three before him "strove in vain". 8) Title "Four Generations": Anshuman is Sagar's grandson, the "son of Asamanj" (Canto XLII). So four men span five generations, with Asamanj skipped. Say "four men of one family". Correct details: Shiva standing "upon the lofty crest / That crowns the Lord of Snow", Ganga as "daughter of the Lord of Snow", and Ganga "whose waves in Swarga flow".
check.safety: Not safe as a bedtime Reel without heavy cuts, and the cuts remove the asana link. Flags: (a) Sixty thousand sons are burned "to heaps of ashes", a mass death at the core of the plot. While digging, "Innumerable creatures die" and they "their guiltless blood they spill". (b) The whole goal is funeral rites, washing the dead. (c) Indra steals the horse in demon disguise, which shows a god badly. (d) Ganga, a sacred goddess, rages and wants to whirl Shiva "To hell's profoundest deep" until "her pride were tamed". This shows a goddess badly and must be left out. (e) The sage Jahnu drinks up the river in anger (Canto XLIV). Leave it out. (f) Sagar, Anshuman, Dilipa and Bhagiratha are all kings. These are myth kings, not real monarchy, but the strict no-royalty rule still flags them. (g) The austerities are extreme: one toe for a year, five fires, a fast broken once a month. Do not present them as a model for students or children. If any of this is used, keep it to Bhagiratha's patience and treat Kapila, Ganga and Shiva with respect.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The quotes are real and word for word in Griffith's Ramayana, and Kapilasana is on Sweeney's Advanced B list. But Kapila is the one who burns the 60,000 sons to ash, not the one who keeps trying. The story is full of death, and it is about huge hard feats, not small daily steps. Skip it for this Reel, or at most add one caption line that India has a Yu Gong story too: Bhagiratha.

candidates.myth_title: Nala's Bridge and the Little Squirrel
candidates.asana: Setu Bandhasana (link by the name only: setu = bridge, bandha = to bind or build)
candidates.series_claim: Setu Bandhasana is in the Primary series, in the closing part before Urdhva Dhanurasana. I checked this in Boonchu's own asana data (ashtanga-graph.js in this repo) and it matches the standard Primary list. Valmiki uses the same two words for Nala's work: 'babandha sāgare setum' (Yuddha Kanda 22.71, 'built the bridge across the sea'). Be honest: no text says the Ashtanga asana was named after Rama's bridge. The link is the shared words. Nala and the squirrel have no asana of their own. Hanumanasana is already used.
candidates.source: (1) Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda sarga 22, verses 66-71 (the bridge grows each day; Nala is Vishvakarma's son), English tr. on valmikiramayan.net (copyright 2004 K. M. K. Murthy, NOT public domain). Griffith's Book VI Canto XXII is a red link on Wikisource and I could not open it. There is NO squirrel in this sarga: I checked the English and Sanskrit. (2) The oldest squirrel text I found is Thondaradippodi Alvar, Tirumalai verse 27 (Tamil, Naalayira Divya Prabandham, c. 8th century by tradition per Wikipedia), with word meanings by T. N. Krishnan on divyaprabandham.koyil.org (2016). Search pages also name the Telugu Ranganatha Ramayanam. I did NOT open that, Kamba Ramayanam or Krittivasi, so I make no claim about them. Rama stroking the squirrel and leaving three stripes is folk telling: I found it only on kids' and blog sites.
candidates.key_quote: "On the first day, fourteen Yojanas of bridge were constructed by the monkeys speedily, thrilled with delight as they were, resembling elephants." (Yuddha Kanda 22.66, valmikiramayan.net tr.). Days 2 to 5 (verses 67-70) add 20, 21, 22 and 23 yojanas. Tamil, Tirumalai 27: "குரங்குகள் மலையை நூக்கக் குளித்துத் தாம் புரண்டிட்டோடித் தரங்க நீரடைக்கலுற்ற சலமிலா அணிலம் போலேன்" (word meanings on koyil.org: monkeys pushing mountains; immersing in water; rolling in the sand on the shore; squirrels. The poet says 'I am not like' that squirrel.)
candidates.story_plain: Rama needed a bridge over the wide sea. A monkey named Nala knew how to build it, because his father was the builder of the gods. All the monkeys carried big rocks and trees and dropped them into the water. On the first day, the bridge grew a little. On the next day it grew a bit more, and the day after that a bit more again. On the fifth day, it touched the other shore. An old Tamil song says a tiny squirrel helped too. It dipped in the sea, rolled in the sand, and shook the sand into the gaps. Its help was small, but it came back again and again.
candidates.link_to_theme: Very close parallel. Valmiki gives a number for each day: 14, 20, 21, 22, 23 yojanas, so the bridge grows a little more every day, the way a student grows. The squirrel is the twin of a detail in the Liezi: the widow's little boy, '始齔，跳往助之' (just losing his milk teeth, he skipped along to help). Both stories say no helper is too small. The Alvar's verse is a teacher's line: he is sorry he did not even do the squirrel's small work. For Boonchu's message, the monkeys are the big asanas everyone sees. The squirrel is the little technique that fills the gaps and makes the bridge strong.
candidates.practice_lesson: Build Setu Bandhasana the way the bridge was built: a little more each day. First keep the hands on the floor and lift only a little, with the feet pressing and the legs working. Over weeks, add a bit more weight on the head. Cross the arms only when the neck is ready. Each small grain of sand is one steady breath in the asana.
candidates.safety_flags: WAR: Rama builds the bridge to cross to Lanka for the battle with Ravana. Leave this out completely. Say only that Rama needed to cross the sea. CRIME: Sita being carried off is a kidnapping, so leave it out. Also leave out Rama threatening the Ocean with his arrows (sargas 21-22). The three stripes on the squirrel's back are folk telling: say 'people say', not 'the Ramayana says'. Setu Bandhasana puts weight on the neck, so the lesson must stress going slowly. Copyright: the English for 22.66 is a modern copyrighted translation. Quote it briefly with credit, or paraphrase.

check.corrected_quote: Use the public-domain Griffith lines first. They are free of copyright and I checked them word for word: "Ere set of sun, so toiled each crew, / Ten leagues and four the structure grew; / The labours of the second day / Gave twenty more of ready way, / And on the fifth, when sank the sun, / The whole stupendous work was done." (Valmiki, tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Ramayan of Valmiki, Book VI, Canto XXII "Ocean Threatened", 1870-74, Project Gutenberg eBook #24869). Griffith skips days 3 and 4. For all five numbers, the Murthy English for 22.66 is also exact: "On the first day, fourteen Yojanas of bridge were constructed by the monkeys speedily, thrilled with delight as they were, resembling elephants." (K. M. K. Murthy, valmikiramayan.net, (c) January 2004). Verses 67-70 give 20, 21, 22 and 23. Together that is 100 yojanas, the full length given in 22.74. The Sanskrit 22.71 "babandha sagare setum" is exact. Verse 22.76 is an even better name link because it has the very compound: "dadrishuh sarva bhutani sagare setu bandhanam" (all beings saw the bridge-building in the sea). The Tamil Tirumalai 27, lines 1-2, also matches koyil.org exactly: "குரங்குகள் மலையை நூக்கக் குளித்துத் தாம் புரண்டிட்டோடித் தரங்க நீரடைக்கலுற்ற சலமிலா அணிலம் போலேன்". The page glosses it as "(I am) not like the squirrels", in the plural. The two tied lines to use: Liezi 5 has Yugong say the wise man "曾不若孀妻弱子" (is not even like the widow and her weak child). The Alvar says he is "not like the squirrels". Each one shames the grown-up with the smallest helper.
check.corrected_source: (1) Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda sarga 22. Verses 44-51: the Ocean names Nala, son of Vishvakarma, and Nala says he can build. Verses 66-70: the five days. Verses 71 and 76: the words babandha/setu bandhanam. English: Griffith 1870-74, Book VI Canto XXII (public domain, Gutenberg #24869; it opens fine there even though Wikisource is a red link). Also K. M. K. Murthy, valmikiramayan.net, (c) Jan 2004 (copyrighted). Neither has a squirrel. I searched all of Griffith for "squirrel" and found 0 hits. (2) Squirrel: Thondaradippodi Alvar, Tirumalai pasuram 27, Tamil, in the Naalayira Divya Prabandham. Wikipedia gives his date as 8th century AD. The English word meanings and commentary are by tnkrishnan (signed "krishNa ramanuja dasan") on divyaprabandham.koyil.org, 25 Oct 2016. The series index says the translation is "based on periyavAchchAn piLLai's vyAkhyAnam". Periyavachchan Pillai is a later Srivaishnava teacher. The details of shaking sand into the gaps and doing it over and over come from that COMMENTARY, not from the verse. (3) Rama stroking the squirrel and giving it three stripes is folk telling only. I found no source for it.
check.asana_series_confirmed: Yes. Setu Bandhasana is the last asana of the Primary series. It comes right after Urdhva Mukha Paschimottanasana and before Urdhva Dhanurasana and the finishing asanas. I confirmed this in /home/user/aybkk-workshop/ashtanga-graph.js line 81, where it is the last Primary entry before the "FINISHING ASANAS" block, and on ashtanga.yoga/primary-series, which gives the same order. The name link is honest only as "the same words". No source I opened says the Ashtanga asana was named after Rama's bridge. Monier-Williams gives the root bandh as both "construct (a dam or a bridge)" and "assume (a posture)", so the double meaning is real. Valmiki 22.76 "setu bandhanam" is the closest wording. Nala and the squirrel have no asana of their own.
check.story_errors: 1) "On the first day, the bridge grew a little": FALSE. Day 1 was 14 yojanas. Murthy glosses a yojana as about 8 miles, and Griffith says "Ten leagues and four". The work was done "speedily" by monkeys "resembling elephants". It was not a little. 2) "The next day a bit more, and the day after that a bit more again": the numbers do rise (14, 20, 21, 22, 23), but the whole 100 yojanas was done in five days by "thousand crores of monkeys" (22.77), "with a great speed" (22.69). The source story is about speed and huge strength, not slow small steps. Yugong is the opposite: his family makes one round trip per season (寒暑易節，始一反焉) and plans across endless generations. 3) "his father was the builder of the gods": sarga 22 only says son of Vishvakarma and equal to him. "Architect of the Gods" is Griffith's footnote gloss. It is fine as a gloss, but it is not in the verse. 4) "Nala knew how to build it": in the source, the Ocean god names him first. Nala then says he had not spoken of his skill because nobody asked him (Griffith: "But why unbidden should I fill / Thine ear with praises of my skill?"). This is a nice humble-teacher detail if wanted. 5) "a tiny squirrel": koyil.org and the commentary say "squirrels", plural ("Some squirrels"). 6) "shook the sand into the gaps" and "came back again and again": these are NOT in the Tamil song. They come from Periyavachchan Pillai's commentary ("shake their bodies so that sand would fall off... By repeating these steps"). Say "an old teacher who explained the song says", not "an old Tamil song says". 7) link_to_theme is wrong where it says the squirrel "fills the gaps and makes the bridge strong". The same commentary says "whatever these squirrels do cannot help even an iota in blocking the ocean" and "the few grains of sand carried by them would not help in filling up the gaps". Its worth is a pure heart that wants no reward (salam ila) and, in an alternate reading, steadiness. 8) "the Alvar's verse is a teacher's line" is not supported. It is a devotee's confession to Ranganatha ("I am not even like the squirrels"). 9) The practice_lesson is reasonable. It uses "asana" correctly and has no long dash.
check.safety: LEAVE OUT, all in Valmiki sarga 22 or around it: (a) the war purpose. 22.79 has Vibhishana with a mace "for the purpose of invading the enemies", and the army then marches. (b) Sita's abduction. (c) Rama threatening the Ocean and shooting the Brahma arrow, the Ocean giving way "in fear of punishment" (22.48), and Nala's line "It yields to naught but punishment" in Griffith. (d) Griffith's lines calling the Abhira people "vile in act as foul of face, fierce Dasyus", and Rama drying up their lands. These are ethnic slurs and must never be quoted. (e) In the koyil.org commentary: Rama's line about burning lust (kAmAgni) and the image of the bow and arrows. (f) The Alvar's life story on the koyil.org index (a courtesan, a king jailing him). Do not tell it. Thailand: Thai kings are styled "Rama", and the Thai Ramakien is tied to King Rama I. Tell it from Valmiki and the Tamil song only. Do not call Rama "the king", do not use Ramakien names or Wat Phra Kaew images, and do not link it to the Thai monarchy. The three stripes are folk telling: say "people say". Never mock the squirrels as useless. Keep the source's tone: the Lord saw their good hearts. Body: Setu Bandhasana loads the neck, so keep the slow, step-by-step lesson. Copyright: Murthy's English is (c) 2004, so quote Griffith (public domain) instead or paraphrase.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The quotes are real, and Setu Bandhasana is in the Primary series. But a huge army of monkeys built the bridge fast, in just five days, so it is not a slow story. The old teacher who explains the squirrel says its sand did not really help, so tell it as a small, kind helper who kept going, like the widow's little boy who helped the Foolish Old Man.

candidates.myth_title: Bhagiratha Brings the Ganga Down (four generations, one river)
candidates.asana: Kapilasana (sage Kapila is in the story); weaker second link: Viranchyasana A/B (Viranchi = Brahma, who grants the wish). There is NO Bhagirathasana in Ashtanga.
candidates.series_claim: There is no Bhagirathasana in any Ashtanga series. I checked Primary, Intermediate and Advanced A in Boonchu's ashtanga-graph.js, and Advanced B in Kino MacGregor's list (yogaphotography.com). 'Bhagirathasana' shows up outside Ashtanga as a modern name for a tree-like one-leg standing asana. I saw that only in a LinkedIn post, so it is weak. Kapilasana IS in Advanced B: Kino's list runs Mula Bandhasana, Nahusasana A-C, Vrschikasana, Sayanasana, Buddhasana, Kapilasana. Viranchyasana A/B are in Advanced A (repo list). Garuda also appears in this story (Canto XLII), but Garudasana is not in any of the four series. Also checked, with no asana link: Upamanyu, Aruni and Ekalavya (Ekalavya ends with a cut thumb, so not for bedtime). Kashyapa's legend of draining the Kashmir lake I skipped, because Kashmir is political. Krouncha's story starts with a hunter killing a bird. Viranchi's 'tapa tapa' (Bhagavata Purana 2.9): I saw only the copyrighted Prabhupada translation. For these I did not open primary texts.
candidates.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda, Griffith's Book I Cantos XL-XLIV (the sons dig, Kapil, Sagar's Sacrifice, Bhagirath, The Descent of Gangá). Tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, 1870-74, public domain. Opened on Wikisource, rendered page and raw text. The Mahabharata Vana Parva version (Ganguli, sections 106-109) I did NOT open: sacred-texts gave 403 and Gutenberg's copy cut off early. I saw only an auto-made wisdomlib summary. The idea that the Sanskrit idiom 'Bhagiratha prayatna' means 'Bhagiratha's labour' comes from Wikipedia (secondary).
candidates.key_quote: "The fervent king a year remained / With arms upraised, refusing rest / While with one toe the earth he pressed" (Griffith, Book I Canto XLIV). Also verified, Canto XLIII: "Thousands of years he thus endured / Till Brahmá's favour was assured" and "For earth alone will never bear / Those torrents hurled from upper air". Canto XLII, about Sagar: "He pondered long with anxious thought / But saw no way to what he sought."
candidates.story_plain: Long ago, a family wanted to bring the river Ganga down from the sky. The great-great-grandfather, Sagar, thought for many years but found no way. His grandson Anshuman tried hard, but the river did not come. Anshuman's son Dilipa tried too, and still the river did not come. Then came Dilipa's son, Bhagiratha. He knew the work was now his turn. He stood on one toe with his arms up for a whole year. At last the river began to fall, and the god Shiva caught her in his long hair, so she would not break the earth. Then Ganga flowed gently behind Bhagiratha, all the way to the sea.
candidates.link_to_theme: The closest Indian twin of the Foolish Old Man. Yugong says '子子孫孫，無窮匱也' (sons and grandsons, without end). Bhagiratha's family really did that: Sagar, Anshuman, Dilipa, then Bhagiratha. Each one's effort looked like failure, but it was one more basket of earth. Both stories end with heaven helping. In the Liezi, '帝感其誠' (the Emperor of Heaven was moved by his sincerity). Here Brahma grants the wish and Shiva holds the river. For Boonchu: a student may not see the result this year, but no day of practice is wasted. Each day stands on the days before.
candidates.practice_lesson: Shiva caught the river in his hair because 'earth alone will never bear / Those torrents hurled from upper air.' A big opening in the body must come down slowly too. In Kapilasana, or in any deep asana, take a little each day. A sudden flood of depth breaks the 'earth': knees, back, shoulders. For a beginner audience, Boonchu can show Bhagiratha's one-toe year with a simple steady one-leg balance and five quiet breaths, without calling it Bhagirathasana.
candidates.safety_flags: LEAVE OUT: Sagar's 60,000 sons dig through the earth killing creatures (Canto XL: 'Of monsters dying 'neath their blows'). They charge at Kapil shouting 'Stand, villain! stand!' and are burnt to ashes (Canto XLI). The river is needed to wash their ashes, so in a bedtime version say only 'to help the family'. Leave out the horse sacrifice. Kapila must not look cruel: either skip him or say only that he was a great sage. ROYALTY: Bhagiratha, Sagar and Dilipa are mythic kings. Keep crowns and palaces out and just use their names. Jahnu drinking the river in anger is optional; skip it. Speak of Ganga with respect: she is a goddess to many viewers.

check.corrected_quote: All four quotes in the claim match Griffith word for word. Main quote, Canto XLIV: "The fervent king a year remained / With arms upraised, refusing rest / While with one toe the earth he pressed, / Still as a post, with sleepless eye". These lines carry the theme better, both verified in Canto XLIV. Brahma: "Then Ans'umán, dear Prince! although / No brighter name the world could show, / Strove long the heavenly flood to gain / To visit earth, but strove in vain." The river stuck in Shiva's hair: "Bhagirath saw it, and anew / His penance dire began." Canto XLIII: "Thousands of years he thus endured / Till Brahmá's favour was assured" and "For earth alone will never bear / Those torrents hurled from upper air" (Brahma says these lines, not the narrator). Canto XLII, Sagar: "He pondered long with anxious thought / But saw no way to what he sought." Liezi lines checked against the Hong Kong EDB school edition (a secondary edition, Chinese only): "子子孫孫，無窮匱也" and "帝感其誠".
check.corrected_source: Valmiki Ramayana, Book I (Bala Kanda), Cantos XL to XLIV, tr. Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Rámáyan of Válmíki (1870-74), public domain. Read on English Wikisource as raw wikitext. The Advanced B list is not "Kino MacGregor's list". It is Richard Pilnick's photo page "Ashtanga Yoga Advanced B photography with Kino MacGregor" (yogaphotography.com, copyright Richard Pilnick). Viranchi as a name of Brahma: Apte, Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary, quoted on wisdomlib ("Virañci.—Name of Brahman."). The Mahabharata Vana Parva version is still unopened, so do not cite it. The 'Bhagiratha prayatna' idiom is still Wikipedia-only, so leave it out or call it secondary.
check.asana_series_confirmed: Kapilasana: confirmed in Advanced B, 8th, after Buddhasana and before Akarna Dhanurasana A, on Richard Pilnick's yogaphotography.com page (the photos are of Kino MacGregor). Viranchyasana A and B: confirmed in Advanced A in /home/user/aybkk-workshop/ashtanga-graph.js lines 165-166. Extra option: Natarajasana (repo spells it 'Natrajasana', Advanced A, line 175). Nataraja is Shiva, and Portland Art Museum says of a Nataraja image: "The Goddess Ganga is enmeshed in Shiva's hair." There is no Bhagirathasana in any series. No source says any of these asanas was named after this story, so say 'the same name' (Kapila, Viranchi/Brahma, Nataraja/Shiva) and never 'named after'. The Kapila link is the weakest: in Griffith, Kapil is Vasudeva/Vishnu "in Kapil's form", and his only act is burning the 60,000 sons, which must be cut. Once that is cut, Kapila does nothing in the bedtime version. Brahma (Viranchi) is the cleaner link because he grants the wish and praises Bhagiratha.
check.story_errors: 1) Title says 'four generations'. The family line is Sagar, then Asamanj, then Ansuman, then Dilipa, then Bhagiratha. That is five generations, and four of them tried. Say 'four tries, one family' or 'five generations'. 2) 'He knew the work was now his turn' is made up. The source says only "on one wish, one thought intent, / Planning the heavenly stream's descent". 3) Big gap: before the one-toe year, Bhagiratha practised for "Thousands of years" at Gokarna to win Brahma (Canto XLIII). The one-toe year (Canto XLIV) came after Brahma said yes, and it was to win Shiva. The story skips the long daily part, which is the best part for the theme. 4) Gap: after Shiva caught her, Ganga was lost in his hair "many lengthening seasons". Bhagiratha "anew / His penance dire began" before Shiva let her go. He had to start again after the win. The story leaves this out. 5) 'Ganga flowed gently' is not in the source. It says "down in all their might they burst / And roared along the ground". Calm parts come later, and she floods Jahnu's ground on the way. Say 'followed him'. 6) 'so she would not break the earth' is close enough to Brahma's "earth alone will never bear". 7) Link_to_theme overreaches. 'Each one's effort was one more basket of earth' and 'no day is wasted' are not in the text. Brahma says Ansuman "strove in vain", says Dilipa did not bring her, and gives the success to Bhagiratha alone ("But thou, O King, earned success"). The honest parallel is that the wish was handed down and never dropped, like Yugong's sons and grandsons. Do not say the earlier tries added up. Everything else checks out: Sagar found no way (30,000 years), Ansuman did penance on the Himalaya, Dilipa failed, and Ganga reached the sea.
check.safety: The claim's cut list is right and checks out word for word ("Of monsters dying 'neath their blows", Canto XL; "Stand, villain! stand!" and the burning to ashes, Canto XLI). Also cut these: (a) Indra steals the horse "in demon guise" (Canto XL). It shows a god as a thief, so skip it. (b) Kapil is Vishnu in Kapil's form. Showing him burning 60,000 youths shows a god in anger, so never tell it. (c) Ganga's "wrath", her "haughty" pride, her wish to sweep Shiva "To hell's profoundest deep", and "until her pride were tamed". Telling these could disrespect a goddess, so leave them all out. (d) Bhagiratha's five fires, eating once a month and sleeping in a winter brook are extreme self-denial. Children should not copy them. Say only 'he practised every day for a very long time'. (e) Ashes, funeral offerings and a sacrifice: say only 'to help his family'. (f) Jahnu drinking the river in anger: skip it. (g) A royalty link the claim missed. Valmiki tells this tale to Rama about Rama's own ancestors (Ikshvaku's line, "Thus, Ráma, I at length have told"). Thai kings carry the title Rama. Never call them Rama's ancestors and never name the Ikshvaku line. Keep Sagar, Dilipa and Bhagiratha as names only: no crowns, no palace, no chariot (he rides "a car of heavenly frame"). (h) Keep the river's fall calm and safe so it does not look like a flood disaster.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The quotes are real and match Griffith's Ramayana word for word. Fix the story: Bhagiratha first practised for thousands of years, then stood on one toe for a year, and he started again when the river got stuck in Shiva's hair. Kapila only burns people here, so link this story to Viranchyasana (Brahma) instead, and say "the same name", not "named after".

candidates.myth_title: The Mother Hen and the Worn Handle (the Buddha's story of unseen daily progress)
candidates.series_claim: Kukkutasana is in the Primary series, right after Garbha Pindasana. It is in the repo's ashtanga-graph.js as 'Kukutasana'. Urdhva Kukkutasana A/B/C are in Advanced A (repo). Pungu Kukkutasana is in Advanced B (Kino MacGregor list). The link is a word link: the Pali text uses kukkuṭī (hen) and kukkuṭapotakā (chicks), and the asana name kukkuṭa means rooster. The Buddha's story is not about the asana.
candidates.source: Samyutta Nikaya 22.101, Vāsijaṭa Sutta ('The Adze'). English tr. Bhikkhu Sujato (SuttaCentral, released CC0, public domain). Pali root text from SuttaCentral's bilara-data on GitHub. Note: this is a teaching simile from the Pali Canon, not a myth.
candidates.key_quote: "They don't know how much of the handle was worn away today, how much yesterday, and how much previously. They just know what has been worn away." (SN 22.101, segments 6.2-6.4, tr. Sujato). Hen: "Suppose there was a chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs. And she properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated." (5.1-5.2). Pali: 'kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vā' (3.1).
candidates.story_plain: One day the Buddha told a little story about a mother hen. She had eight, ten or twelve eggs. Every day she sat on them and kept them warm. She did not need to wish, 'Oh, I hope my chicks come out!' Because she sat well, the chicks broke their shells all by themselves. Then the Buddha told about a builder and his tool with a wooden handle. Every day his fingers rubbed the handle a tiny bit. He could never see how much wore away today, or yesterday. But one day he looked, and there were his finger marks, deep in the wood.
candidates.link_to_theme: This is the Reel's theme in the Buddha's own words: small daily work you cannot see, adding up to something you can. It matches Yugong, who could carry only one basket at a time. One round trip took a whole season ('寒暑易節，始一反焉'), yet the mountain would still go. The hen does not wish, she sits. Boonchu's students do not need to wish for the next asana; they come and do the little technique. The Primary sequence even tells it in order: Garbha Pindasana (the baby in the egg) comes just before Kukkutasana (the chick). The same sutta has a ship's ropes worn by weather (6.7) if a second picture is needed.
candidates.practice_lesson: Roll in Garbha Pindasana every day and do not count progress. Like the handle, you will not see what changed today or yesterday. Then one day the rolling stops on the hands, and you lift into Kukkutasana. Sit on your eggs: come to the mat on the days when nothing seems to change.
candidates.safety_flags: Clean for bedtime. Not a myth, so frame it as 'a story the Buddha told'. Keep the Buddha's point respectful: in the sutta the hatching stands for freeing the mind, not for getting an asana. Say the asana use is Boonchu's lesson, not the Buddha's. Both asanas need full lotus: never force the knees, and use the 'slow handle' message here too.

check.corrected_quote: Adze (SN 22.101, 6.1 to 6.4, tr. Sujato): "Suppose a mason or their apprentice sees the marks of his fingers and thumb on the handle of his adze. They don’t know how much of the handle was worn away today, how much yesterday, and how much previously. They just know what has been worn away." Hen (5.1 to 5.5): "Suppose there was a chicken with eight or ten or twelve eggs. And she properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated. That chicken might not wish: ‘If only my chicks could break out of the eggshell with their claws and beak and hatch safely!’ But still they can break out and hatch safely." Pali (5.1, same words also at 3.1): "Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kukkuṭiyā aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vā." Chicks = kukkuṭapotakā (5.4). All three match the source word for word; the claim's quotes were correct (only straight vs curly apostrophes differ).
check.corrected_source: Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.101, Vāsijaṭa Sutta ("The Adze"), Linked Discourses 22, chapter 10 "Flowers", spoken at Sāvatthī to the monks. English tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral bilara-data (dedicated to the public domain under CC0; confirmed in bilara-data LICENSE.md). Hen simile segments 3.1 to 3.8 (hen that did not sit well) and 5.1 to 5.8 (hen that did); adze simile 6.1 to 6.6; ship ropes 6.7 to 6.8. Pali root: SuttaCentral Mahāsaṅgīti text (root/pli/ms). No year is given in the files, so do not print a year. This is a teaching simile ("Suppose..."), not a myth.

check.asana_series_confirmed: Kukkutasana in Primary, right after Garbha Pindasana: CONFIRMED (repo ashtanga-graph.js lines 73-74 "Garbha Pindasana" then "Kukutasana"; ashtangayoga.info Primary page lists Garbha Pindasana then Kukkutasana, and names Kukkutasana "Hahn" = rooster). The repo lists "Punga Kukutasana" in public/asana-info.json with no series, and the Kino page I tried redirected elsewhere. Leave it out of the Reel or check it before use. But link_to_theme breaks this twice: it calls Kukkutasana "the chick" (wrong, it is the rooster) and calls Garbha Pindasana "the baby in the egg" (wrong: garbha = womb or embryo; the repo itself labels it "Womb Embryo", ashtangayoga.info "Eingerollter Embryo"). The egg-to-chick order is a nice teacher's picture only if Boonchu says it is his own picture, not the meaning of the names.
check.story_errors: 1) "Every day she sat on them" is NOT in the text. The sutta says she "properly sat on them" (sammā adhisayitāni). "Every day" is the Reel's theme pushed into the Buddha's mouth. Say "She sat on them well, the right way." 2) "the chicks broke their shells all by themselves": the text says they "can break out and hatch safely" with "their claws and beak". Say "the chicks could break out with their little claws and beaks." 3) "a builder and his tool with a wooden handle": source is "a mason or their apprentice" and "the handle of his adze" (Pali palagaṇḍa, vāsijaṭa). "Builder" is OK as simple English; "wooden" is added. 4) "Every day his fingers rubbed the handle a tiny bit" is an inference, not a line in the text. The text only says some was worn "today, yesterday, and previously". 5) "But one day he looked, and there were his finger marks, deep in the wood": "one day he looked", "deep" and "wood" are all added. The text: he "sees the marks of his fingers and thumb on the handle". Also add the thumb. 6) "One day the Buddha told a little story": it is a "Suppose..." picture told to monks at Sāvatthī, not a story with events. check.safety: Clean for bedtime: no violence, no adult content, no politics or royalty. The negative hen case only says the chicks "can't break out and hatch safely". In a kids' version do not say or show chicks dying. The ship ropes "rot away" is fine. Respect points: (a) frame it as "a picture the Buddha gave his monks", not a myth or fairy tale; (b) say clearly that in the sutta the hatching stands for the mind being freed (ending of defilements), and that the asana lesson is Boonchu's, not the Buddha's; (c) because Boonchu is in Thailand, do not use a Buddha statue or image as a casual prop near feet, on the mat, or in a playful edit. Do not mention Pungu Kukkutasana ("wounded rooster") unless its series is checked first.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The Buddha's adze line is real and word for word: you cannot see what wore away today or yesterday, you only see the marks. It is a perfect partner for Yugong's mountain. Please fix two things: the hen "sat on them well" (the text does not say "every day"), and Kukkutasana means rooster, not chick, while Garbha Pindasana means a baby in the womb, not in an egg.

candidates.myth_title: The Fisherman Who Listened Inside the Fish for Twelve Years (Matsyendra)
candidates.series_claim: Ardha Matsyendrasana is in the Intermediate series, after Bharadvajasana. Purna Matsyendrasana is in Advanced A. Both are in the repo's ashtanga-graph.js (Intermediate and 'Advance A'). The name link is direct: Matsyendra means 'Lord of the Fishes'.
candidates.source: Oldest layer: the Kaulajñānanirṇaya (attributed to Matsyendra, c. 11th century), as summarised in P. C. Bagchi's English introduction (Calcutta Sanskrit Series III, 1934, pp. 8-9; archive.org DLI scan, OCR). That version is a DIFFERENT story: Kārttikeya steals the scripture and throws it into the sea, a fish swallows it, and Bhairava as a fisherman kills the fish to get it back ('This Brahmin is called Matsyaghna as he killed the fish'). The listening-fish version: Bagchi p. 16 gives it from the Skandapurāṇa, Nāgarakhaṇḍa. The 'twelve years inside the fish' detail: Abhayadatta's Lives of the 84 Mahasiddhas (12th century, kept in Tibetan), story of Mīnapa. I saw this ONLY in a secondary summary by the Tibetan Buddhist Resource Center on Google Arts & Culture, not in a translation. Wikipedia also gives twelve years and lists Minapa as one of Matsyendra's names.
candidates.key_quote: Bagchi 1934, p. 16 (OCR, summarising the Skandapurāṇa legend): "The fish then related how he was born in the Gandantayoga, thrown into the sea and swallowed by a fish and how, on overhearing the conversations of Siva and Parvati had attained Jñānayoga." (The OCR reads 'sca' and 'Jiinayoga'.) Secondary only, on the 12 years (TBRC/Google Arts & Culture): "practicing for twelve years inside the leviathan before being cut free by a fellow fisherman".
candidates.story_plain: A fisherman went out to sea, and a giant fish swallowed him. Deep under the water, the god Shiva was teaching the goddess Parvati the secrets of yoga. Inside the fish, the fisherman heard every word. He kept very still and listened. Then he practiced what he heard, a little each day. He did this for twelve years, in the dark, where no one could see him. At last other fishermen caught the big fish and set him free. He stepped out as a great yogi, and people called him Matsyendra, Lord of the Fishes.
candidates.link_to_theme: A parallel on the daily part, with a contrast in style. Yugong's work is loud and seen: baskets, neighbours, a laughing wise man. Matsyendra's work is quiet and unseen: twelve years of listening and practicing where nobody watches. Both say the big change comes from keeping on. For Boonchu: the student who listens closely to one small cue, every day, for years, becomes the teacher later. Weaker on 'many small efforts building one big thing' than Bhagiratha or the bridge.
candidates.practice_lesson: In Ardha Matsyendrasana, do not crank the twist with the arm. Listen like the fish: on each exhale turn a tiny bit more, then stay still for the breath. Do five breaths every practice, for months. Purna Matsyendrasana in Advanced A is the twelve-year version: it needs the lotus to come first.
candidates.safety_flags: LEAVE OUT: the oldest version kills the fish to get the scripture back. A later legend has a baby thrown into the sea because he was born under a bad star (Bagchi p. 16, Wikipedia). Later Nath tales have Parvati angry and cursing him, and his stay in Kadali, the land of women (adult). A man swallowed by a fish can scare small children, so tell it softly. SOURCE CAUTION: 'twelve years' is not in Bagchi's Skandapurāṇa summary. It is in the Mīnapa tale per a secondary summary, so say 'the old tales say'. A popular detail, that Parvati fell asleep and the fisherman answered 'yes, I understand', I saw only in a search snippet with no named source: do not use it unless Boonchu checks Dowman's Masters of Mahamudra (1985, copyrighted). Hindu Nath and Tibetan Buddhist traditions both honour this figure (Tibet links him with Avalokiteshvara), so do not pick a side.

But "a little each day" is not in any old text, and the twelve years come only from a short modern museum caption. candidates.myth_title: The Golden Peacock Who Said His Morning Words Every Day (Mora Jataka, No. 159)
candidates.series_claim: Mayurasana and Pincha Mayurasana are in the Intermediate series (repo ashtanga-graph.js). The name link is honest: Pali 'mora' is the same word as Sanskrit 'mayūra', peacock. The Jataka hero is the peacock itself.
candidates.source: Jataka No. 159, Mora-Jātaka. The Jataka, Vol. II, ed. E. B. Cowell, tr. W. H. D. Rouse, 1895, public domain. Opened on wisdomlib, which labels the whole 6-volume set under Robert Chalmers; Vol. II is in fact Rouse's. The sacred-texts copy (j2012.htm) gave 403 to my fetch.
candidates.key_quote: Morning charm: "There he rises, king all-seeing, / Making all things bright with his golden light. / Thee I worship, glorious being, / Making all things bright with thy golden light". The day he was caught: "leaving his charm unsaid, he came towards her". The hunter "tried for seven years, but catch him he could not".
candidates.story_plain: Long ago, a golden peacock lived on a golden hill. Every morning he watched the sun come up and said his special words. Every evening he watched the sun go down and said his words again. These small words, said every single day, kept him safe. Hunters tried to catch him for years and years, but they never could. One morning, a lovely bird song called him away. He flew off before he said his morning words. That was the only day he was caught. But the wise peacock was not afraid: he taught the people to be kind, and then flew home to his golden hill.
candidates.link_to_theme: A parallel on 'every day' and a contrast on generations. In Yugong, generations of digging win against the mountain. In the Jataka, hunters sent over six kings' reigns fail against one bird's small daily habit. The habit is the strength, and the one skipped day is the only danger. For Boonchu: little techniques done daily keep a student safe and steady. The peacock's words are to the rising sun, so it ties neatly to Surya Namaskara, which opens every Ashtanga practice.
candidates.practice_lesson: Say your morning words: never skip the sun salutations before Mayurasana. Build Mayurasana by tiny daily holds: lift the feet for one breath today, two breaths next week. Do not try for a long hold on one brave day.
candidates.safety_flags: ADULT: he is caught by a trained peahen whose cry 'woke desire' in him. Change this to 'a lovely bird song called him away'. LEAVE OUT: kings want to eat him to stay young forever; the first hunter dies after seven years of trying; the king gives his kingdom to the peacock. ROYALTY: the tale opens 'when Brahmadatta was king of Benares' and has a line of kings. Keep kings out and say 'people' or 'hunters'. The peacock is the Bodhisatta, a past life of the Buddha, so tell it with respect. This matters for a Thai Buddhist audience.

The evening verse (p. 24) begins: "There he sets, the king all-seeing, / He that makes all bright with his golden light." and ends: "Through the night, as through the day, / Keep me safe, I pray." Hunters (p. 24): "This the hunter tried for seven years, but catch him he could not". The day he was caught (p. 25): "leaving his charm unsaid, he came towards her; and was caught in the net."
