check.story_errors: 1) "These small words": the source calls them "a Brahma spell" and a "charm". Each time it is two verses: one to the sun and one honouring the Buddhas of the past. "Small" is the writer's spin. "Special words" is fine. 2) "said every single day": this is implied by the habit-style telling and by the hunter who "observed ... he recited a charm before setting out in search of food". The text never says "every single day". It is a fair inference, but it is not a quote. 3) "a lovely bird song called him away": this hides the key fact. A hunter trained a peahen, set the snare "early in the morning, before the peacock had recited his charm", and made her cry on purpose. It was a planned trap, not chance. A soft version can keep the truth: "a clever hunter used a bird's call to trick him". 4) "He flew off": the source says "he came towards her; and was caught in the net". He did not fly off. 5) "the wise peacock was not afraid": this is not in the source. It was added. 6) "he taught the people to be kind": in the source he teaches the king that everything except Nirvana passes away, and he sets the king in keeping the Five Commandments (precepts). It is not "the people", and it is not "be kind". He first proves his past life as a world ruler by having a lake drained to dig up his jewelled car. The king offers him the kingdom and he gives it back. Changing "the king" to "the people" alters the source to dodge the royalty rule. Better: end the bedtime version at the catch, or say only "In the end, he flew home to his golden hill." 7) The claim says the tale's lesson is daily practice. The Jataka's own lesson is different: the Buddha tells it to a monk who strayed after seeing a well-dressed woman, and the moral is that desire makes even the wise fall in a moment. The "daily steps" reading is Boonchu's own angle and should be framed as that. 8) link_to_theme says "hunters sent over six kings' reigns fail". That matches the text ("the kingdom was ruled by six successive kings. Then a seventh arose"), but it is for internal notes only.
check.safety: FAIL as written, PASS with cuts. ROYALTY: kings run through the whole tale. It opens with Brahmadatta, king of Benares. Queen Khema's dream starts the hunt. Seven kings in a row send hunters. The peacock says he once "held imperial sway over the whole world". The king offers him the kingdom. Ananda is named as the king. Only the first half (sun words, failed hunters, one skipped morning, the catch) can be told without royalty. Do not move the king's role onto "the people". If the verse goes on screen, its "king all-seeing" means the sun. That is low risk, but a voice-over can say "the sun" instead. I found nothing tying the Mora Jataka to Thai royalty, so it is not like the Mahajanaka. DEATH and VIOLENCE (leave out): the first hunter dies after seven years, Queen Khema dies, each later hunter "died in the quest", and the kings want to eat the peacock's flesh to stay young forever. ADULT (leave out): the peahen's cry "woke desire in the peacock's breast". The frame story is also unsafe: the Buddha tells it to a monk who strayed "on hearing a woman's voice", with lines like "What wonder that womankind should trouble the wits of a man like you". That reads as anti-women today. Leave the frame out entirely, and the claim's safety_flags missed it. DATED WORDING: "a savage who lived in a certain village of wild huntsmen". Do not repeat it. RELIGION: the peacock is the Bodhisatta, the Buddha in a past life, and these verses are the Mora Paritta. It is a protective chant still used in Thai Theravada chanting books (it is in the Thai-tradition Chanting Guide on dhammatalks.org). Thai viewers will know it. Do not call it a "magic spell" for laughs. Do not say Surya Namaskara is the same as the paritta. Do not suggest that skipping practice brings bad luck. Tell it with respect.
check.plain_note_for_boonchu: The quotes are real. They are from Rouse's 1895 English Jataka, Vol. II, story 159, and the peacock goes with Mayurasana by the same name only. Tell only the first half: he says his sun words every morning and every evening, the hunters fail for years, and the one morning he skips them, he is caught. Leave out the kings, the deaths and the "desire" part. Remember that the Buddhist lesson of this tale is about desire, so "a little every day" is your own angle on it.

candidates.myth_title: The Parrot Who Carried Water to the Mountain Fire (Chinese Buddhist parable)
candidates.asana: None. No parrot (shuka) asana exists in any of the four Ashtanga series.
candidates.series_claim: No asana link. I checked all four series (repo lists for Primary, Intermediate and Advanced A; Kino MacGregor list for Advanced B). The nearest idea, a small bird against something huge, is the Tittibhasana story, which is already used. Do not force a link. Use this only as a framing story or a caption line, not as an asana episode.
candidates.source: 舊雜譬喻經 (Jiu za piyu jing, 'Old Sutra of Assorted Parables'), Taishō vol. 4 no. 206, scroll 1 (卷上), story no. 23. That is the traditional attribution, and some scholars doubt it. A version also appears in the Taiping Guangji, juan 460 '鸚鵡救火'. ctext.org blocked my fetch, so I did not open it.
candidates.key_quote: 「鸚鵡遙見便入水，以羽翅取水飛上空中，以衣毛間水灑之，欲滅大火。如是往來。」…「我由知而不滅也，我曾客是山中，山中百鳥畜獸皆仁善，悉為兄弟，我不忍見之耳。」天神感其至意，則雨滅火也。 (My plain gloss: The parrot dipped into the water and flew up to sprinkle the fire, back and forth. candidates.story_plain: Long ago, a parrot flew to a far mountain and stayed there for a while. All the birds and animals there were kind, like brothers and sisters. Later, the parrot flew back home. Some months after, a big fire started on that mountain. The parrot saw it from far away. It dipped its wings in the river, flew over the fire, and shook down the drops. It flew back and forth, again and again. A sky god called out, 'Silly parrot! How can two wet wings stop such a huge fire?' The parrot said, 'I know I cannot. But they were my friends, and I cannot just watch.' The god was moved by the parrot's true heart, and sent rain to put the fire out.
candidates.link_to_theme: The closest twin of Yugong in the whole search, but with no asana. A tiny creature takes on a hopeless huge task with small repeated trips ('如是往來'). It is also a Chinese-language Buddhist source, which may suit the China audience. Best used in the caption or as a one-line echo after the Foolish Old Man, not as the asana story.
candidates.practice_lesson: No asana-specific lesson, because there is no honest link. As a general lesson: one breath of steady vinyasa is one drop of water. The teacher does not ask you to put out the whole fire today. Bring today's drops.
candidates.safety_flags: DISASTER: a forest fire. Keep it gentle: no animal is hurt in the source, which says only that the fire burned on all four sides. The god's line '咄鸚鵡！汝何以癡' is a scolding, not a joke: keep the god respectful. It is close to the already-used tittibha-and-sea angle, so do not run them near each other. Present the translator attribution as traditional ('an old Chinese Buddhist book').
